title: US military says it has launched weapons into space
snippet: This is the first public acknowledgment that the U.S. military put a space weapon in Earth's orbit.
fullText:
The U.S. military has for the first time acknowledged that it deployed space weapons into Earth’s orbit.

U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, who oversees the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force, said in a speech Monday that the military has “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.”

Meink did not say what the weapons are, what they do, or how many of them have been deployed, but his phrasing was reportedly intentional and “very well thought out.” 

When reached about the disclosure, an Air Force spokesperson told TechCrunch that the weapons are designed to defend the U.S. military “against space-enabled attack.”

Asked about the threats that the Air Force was responding to by launching the weapon, the spokesperson said that the U.S. had been warning about Russian and Chinese weapons testing in space since 2007.

“Due to their actions, it is no longer a question that space is a warfighting domain. Space control is part of how the Joint Force protects national security interests,” the spokesperson said. “The space domain is contested, and we must be able to secure our nation’s interests in space — that is why the Space Force was established as the 6th military service.” 

“Open communication strengthens deterrence, prevents adversary miscalculation, and normalizes space operations alongside the other services,” the spokesperson told TechCrunch.

The deployment comes as China is long known to have operated spacecraft capable of causing damage to other satellites. The U.S. Space Force says Russia is currently developing a satellite “designed to carry a nuclear weapon.”

According to The Times, the U.S. had long disavowed the destruction of satellites in space, as attacks can leave debris that is harmful to other space objects and astronauts.

title: Apple researchers unveil SimpleDesign, a new AI model for protein design
snippet: In a new study, Apple researchers detail SimpleDesign, a streamlined AI model that can jointly generate protein sequences and structures. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new study, Apple researchers detail SimpleDesign, a streamlined AI model that can jointly generate protein sequences and structures. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Last September, Apple researchers published a study titled “SimpleFold: Folding Proteins is Simpler than You Think,” which detailed a streamlined approach to predicting a protein’s 3D structure from its amino acid sequence.

In a nutshell, SimpleFold uses a flow-matching model to generate a protein’s 3D structure directly from its amino acid sequence.

We explained flow matching in more detail here, but the short of it is that the technique starts with a noisy, random basis and learns a relatively direct path toward the final result. That contrasts with diffusion models, which typically work by iteratively removing noise until they reach the final output.

Both techniques are most commonly (or at least historically) associated with image generation, although researchers (including those at Apple) have also explored diffusion models for text and code generation.

Back to SimpleFold, Apple basically paired flow matching with general-purpose Transformer blocks (commonly used in text generation), allowing the model to avoid some of the more computationally expensive techniques typically used by protein-folding models, such as DeepMind’s famous AlphaFold.

Now, Apple researchers have unveiled SimpleDesign, which applies the same push toward simpler, general-purpose architectures explored with SimpleFold to the broader problem of protein design, rather than just predicting a protein’s 3D structure.

SimpleDesign

As Apple’s researchers explain in a new study titled “SimpleDesign: A Joint Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Codesign”:

Existing models often rely on a multi-stage training process where autoencoders that tokenize data into latent representations are trained in a first stage. Secondly, a generative model is trained on the latent representation of the autoencoder(s), i.e. generative modeling in a latent space. We hypothesize that this multi-stage training is not necessary to obtain performant co-design models and thus present SimpleDesign, an effective multi-modal protein design model trained directly in the data space.

In other words, while many existing protein design models rely on a multi-stage process, SimpleDesign learns to generate amino acid sequences and continuous 3D structures in a single end-to-end training process.

Many current protein co-design models work as follows: first, they train a separate model to convert protein structures into discrete representations, or “tokens.” Then, they train a generative model to work with those representations to generate new protein sequences and structures.

SimpleDesign skips that intermediate step, learning directly from paired amino acid sequences and 3D coordinates rather than first compressing protein structures into a separate tokenized representation.

The way Apple researchers trained SimpleDesign is quite interesting.

They started with more than 2 million protein sequence-and-structure pairs, taken primarily from the AFESM dataset, which combines predicted structures from the AlphaFold Database and additional samples.

During training, they corrupted both parts of each pair: while amino acids in the sequence were randomly hidden behind masked tokens, the corresponding 3D structure also had noise added to it.

The researchers would also vary the extent to which each side was scrambled. If the sequence was mostly intact but the structure was heavily corrupted, the task resembled protein folding, and the model had to recover a structure from a known sequence.

By contrast, if the structure was mostly intact but the sequence was heavily masked, it resembled inverse folding. The model then had to generate a sequence capable of producing a given structure.

And when both were partially scrambled, the model learned to work on the two problems simultaneously, effectively training it for protein co-design.

According to the study, SimpleDesign delivered competitive results across protein co-design, structure generation, and sequence generation benchmarks, despite using a much simpler training pipeline.

The researchers also found that SimpleDesign could generate plausible protein structures, and that the amino acid sequences it produced were generally as good as or better than those generated by most competing multimodal models.

Finally, the researchers noted that SimpleDesign’s results are still limited to computer-based evaluations, since the generated proteins were not experimentally tested to confirm that they would actually fold, function, or behave safely in actual biological systems.

Still, the results were quite promising, and the entire study (which naturally goes much more in depth on SimpleDesign’s architecture, training process, benchmarks, and results) is well worth a look.

title: T-Mobile Is the First Carrier to Support Apple’s iPhone Handoff, but It’ll Cost $5 a Month
snippet: The new iOS 27 feature lets you bounce between two iPhones easily, but the carrier is charging for it. And AT&T is staying hands-free for now.
fullText:
The new iPhone Handoff feature in iOS 27 is a clever idea: If you have two iPhones, you can use either one with a single phone number — the system automatically activates your number on whichever phone is unlocked. And like Apple’s Handoff to Mac and iPad, your texts, calls, voicemails and Find My location follow you, too.

At launch, however, the feature is supported only by T-Mobile in the US, and the carrier is charging $5 a month to use it. And while Verizon support is expected by the end of the year, according to Apple, AT&T appears to be sitting this feature out for now.

	

			

iPhone Handoff is similar to what the Apple Watch has done with data for a few generations, where taking off one watch and putting on another automatically switches all of your information, such as activity tracking, to it. For example, some people use one watch during the day — perhaps the rugged Apple Watch Ultra — and switch to a slimmer, older Apple Watch at night, allowing the first to charge for the morning.

But replicating that behavior to the iPhone requires coordination with cellular providers. Each phone’s eSIM needs to be configured for iPhone Handoff by a carrier, and service needs to switch cleanly on the network side.

Ironically, the Apple Watch gets left out of the iPhone Handoff transaction: Your watch remains paired with just one watch, communicating with it via Wi-Fi or cellular (if that’s an option). “If neither is available,” Apple writes, “calls, messages, notifications, certain health and fitness features, Siri AI or other app experiences relayed from your paired iPhone may not be available.”

In its press release about offering the iPhone 18 Pro, T-Mobile writes, “iPhone Handoff is available on any iPhone with iOS 27 via iPhone settings and ready to use from day one on the new iPhone 18 Pro lineup and iPhone Duo. T-Mobile is introducing the feature at $5/month.”

When I reached out to T-Mobile asking about the charge, a spokesperson wrote via email, “The $5/month charge reflects the added service that powers the experience on both devices.”

While iPhone Handoff appears to seamlessly switch your eSIM just by picking up the phone you want to use, it’s not yet clear what else is different with this process versus just transferring your eSIM manually using your iPhone’s settings menu.

Notably absent from Apple’s news was the other major US carrier, AT&T. I contacted a spokesperson there to learn more about the company’s plans for the feature, but it sounds like it’s not a priority.

“While we see that there could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” the spokesperson replied, “our focus remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” They then pointed to “existing eSIM activation and transfer options across compatible devices.”

In addition to T-Mobile, iPhone Handoff is currently supported by Telekom in Germany. The UK carrier EE will also support the feature later this year, according to Apple.

A Verizon representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Comu’s Action Pro is a great meeting recorder that struggles to justify its AI premium
snippet: As my house becomes increasingly strewn with the detritus of parenting, I’ve made the inverse effort to eliminate excess, physical and digital, from my life. As much as it is about control, it’s also about mental health; I already use my phone too much, so adding yet another thing to the backpack, to the pocket, feels anything but additive. more…
fullText:
As my house becomes increasingly strewn with the detritus of parenting, I’ve made the inverse effort to eliminate excess, physical and digital, from my life. As much as it is about control, it’s also about mental health; I already use my phone too much, so adding yet another thing to the backpack, to the pocket, feels anything but additive.

But I’m also aware of the single-use gadget’s pull, increasingly powerful precisely because people are relying too much on their phones. Digicams to augment overly-processed smartphone photos. Writing tablets that feel like paper without the waste. Smart rings and health trackers to reduce notification overload.

And so it is with a product like the Comu Action Pro, a standalone note-taking gadget that attempts to turn a simple idea into something indispensable.

Pixel owners are likely well aware of the superlative built-in Recorder app that’s been around for years, adding features like real-time transcription and translation as it’s matured. The current app is about all you could want from a piece of software that leverages a phone’s built-in microphones.

	

It was with this framing that I undertook the review of a novel gadget category: the AI voice recorder. I’m not entirely unfamiliar with it: I’ve used early versions of Plaud’s NotePin and Note devices in the past, but never for long enough to feel acquainted with them. In response, I wanted to spend enough time with the Comu Action Pro to understand where and how it fits into my life, and why one may feel justified in spending the $180 it currently costs instead of just using the phone they already have in their pocket.

First, the basics: at a thickness of 7mm, it’s a svelte mixture of aluminum and plastic that’s designed to stick magnetically to the back of a compatible phone, like an iPhone or Pixel. (The box comes with a couple of circular magnetic stickers for devices without built-in MagSafe support.) That said, it’s nowhere close to the 3mm dimensions of the Plaud Note and Note Pro. But that additional girth comes with a few benefits: it fits a USB-C port, so you’re not forced to charge it with a proprietary magnetic cable that will almost certainly be missing when you need it most. And it carries a larger battery that pushes recording time to 70 hours, double that of the Plaud Note Pro.

The primary question I ask myself, and am asked by others, when I use the Comu Action Pro is, “Why?” Why do you need a separate piece of hardware when your phone will suffice, particularly in a world of inexpensive or free AI transcription services that can do most of the job? In short, it’s the passivity of it all; you can just leave the Action Pro running in the background whenever you’re going about your day to collect snippets of conversations, or covertly place it on a boardroom table to record a meeting.

The Action Pro has six far-field microphones that pick up voices from distances that phones are just not tuned for. That omnidirectional nature means the actual recordings sound thin and tinny, but the product is not the audio — it’s the data from the audio. Placing the Action Pro on the table in front of me next to my phone and recording the deliberately subdued tones of a conversation I was having showed the form factor’s inherent compromise; it picked up voices from the tables next to me, leading to audio that was basically unusable to listen to. Conversely, my Pixel 11 Pro did a great job isolating our two voices in the recording itself.

I was surprised, then, to discover the Action Pro transcribed our conversation with minimal errors. The company works with a number of AI vendors, including OpenAI and Google, and while it’s usually accurate, it made more errors than the competition.

It’s the “Action” in Comu’s Action Pro the company really wants to emphasize, and it’s what I believe has the largest potential — and the longest way to go to reach it. If you’ve ever used a cloud-based meeting recorder like Granola you’ll know that its primary job is to synthesize what it records into something compelling and useful, a summary that can lead to identifiable action items. From there you can ask it questions about the content or have it draft a follow-up email.

Comu’s Action Pro tries to go one step further by integrating with foundation models like Claude Opus 5 or GPT-5.6 Terra to turn those summaries into more than just emails; you can ask it to create a summary document or even a presentation, choosing from a number of predefined templates. All of this is done through the app, which is poorly designed, making for an awkward experience.

I’ll give you a small example: I had the Comu Action Pro record all 20 minutes of a YouTube video that was playing at a pretty comfortable volume from my Mac Mini’s thin but capable internal speaker. It was a video I watched doing research for this review, attempting to grasp the scope of the AI note taking market, since I’d really only ever heard of and used Plaud’s products.

As a baseline, I also used my Pixel 11 Pro’s Recorder app alongside a Plaud Note. All three were sitting four or so inches from the speaker and there was little ambient noise in the room. After the recording was finished, I compared the transcripts of each recorder for accuracy, and then delved into the post-production aspects of each product. For full transparency, here are links to both Comu’s and Plaud’s outputs from that recording:

Summaries are good on both, but Plaud’s are neater and better organized.

Plaud’s transcript is slightly more accurate.

Ironically, the Action Pro kept referring to Plaud as “Plot” throughout, though that can be traced to the word’s pronunciation by the host.

Plaud’s output included a mind map and a summary image, whereas Comu’s was text-only.

Comu’s custom documents and presentations are basic, hard to read, and rarely useful as standalone assets.

The Comu app is buggy and, in places, poorly translated into English.

The Comu web app is basically unusable in its current state.

The issue I keep returning to is that the Action Pro really only solves a real-world problem. While you can attach it to the back of the phone to record both sides of a conversation (with consent, of course), there’s no mechanism to record or sync web-based meetings. Plaud, being the more mature product, boasts a much better app, a usable web interface, and a desktop app that records and transcribes video calls, usage of which is included even in the free Starter plan.

Comu’s best features are also gated behind a subscription. Unlike Plaud, which provides access to most features for free but limits transcription minutes to 300 on the free Starter tier, Comulytic goes the other way, offering unlimited transcriptions indefinitely and putting its AI workflows, including translation and document generation, behind a $10/month paywall. Access to Anthropic’s Claude model is also limited to paid subscriptions.

Those are the actions meant to be solved by the dedicated AI button that sits above the record button which, when pressed, acts like a voice-powered agent for your work needs. Anything recorded when the button is pressed goes into a general ChatGPT-like stream, where the data source is the transcribed meeting notes. Unfortunately, that’s where the “Action” part of the Action Pro breaks down: the Comu agent is brittle, and doesn’t interface with other parts of the phone. 

For instance, there’s a “Schedule Tasks” prompt that Comu invites you to use, and tapping it pre-fills a number of templates, including “Schedule a deep work block for this week.” I completed the prompt and wrote “Schedule a deep work block for this Friday from 1 to 5 PM,” but at the moment the model isn’t able to connect to my external calendar. 

In fact, as of writing, every calendar- and task-based connection is listed as “Coming soon.” Once these connections are added, Comu’s offering may be more competitive, but given the proliferation of similar services like Gemini Spark, Meta Muse, Town, Poke, and many others, I’m doubtful that most users will be willing to shell out the monthly fee that Comu is asking for.

At its core, the Action Pro is a competent meeting transcriber with some impressive hardware and lackluster software that, at least right now, doesn’t justify its asking price. If you’re looking for something from the company that’s thinner, lighter, and cheaper, and still has some AI capabilities, Comu’s own Note Pro is a decent alternative at under $120. If you need something a bit more full-featured, including better web and desktop support, I’d go with something from Plaud.

					

A competent meeting recorder and digital note taker whose ambitions to be an AI project manager don’t quite work.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Great audio transcription quality

											

Good build quality

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

App is a mess

											

AI features are half-baked or missing entirely

											

AI features require a minimum $10/month subscription

title: The Boox Palma 3 gets stylus support and a sleek redesign
snippet: Nearly two years after the last update to Boox's smartphone-sized black-and-white e-reader, the company announced the Palma 3 with a sleek redesign, new functionality, and a handful of other small updates that may justify its significant price bump depending on how you plan to use it. It still features the same 6.13-inch, 300ppi E Ink Carta screen as its predecessor (which is now quite a few years old), but it's wrapped in a new anodized aluminum frame with a pap … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Nearly two years after the last update to Boox’s smartphone-sized black-and-white e-reader, the company announced the Palma 3 with a sleek redesign, new functionality, and a handful of other small updates that may justify its significant price bump depending on how you plan to use it. While the Palma 2 launched in 2024 for $279.99, the Palma 3 will be $339.99 and is expected to be “available soon.”

The most obvious upgrade for the Palma 3 is the hardware itself. It still features the same 6.13-inch, 300ppi E Ink Carta screen as its predecessor (which is now quite a few years old), but it’s wrapped in a new anodized aluminum frame with a paperlike fiberglass backplate. The Palma 3 looks like a significant upgrade to the Palma line, even if under the hood you’ll find more of the same. The pocketable e-reader is powered by a Qualcomm Q-6690 octa-core processor with 6GB of RAM and 128GB of storage expandable with a microSD card. It also includes a 3950mAh rechargeable battery, a 16-megapixel camera on the back, and a fingerprint reader in the power button.

The original Palma and the Palma 2 came with Android 11 and Android 13, respectively, but the new Palma 3 ships with Android 16, which is just one generation behind the latest version of the OS. That should help it feel like a more modern mobile device. And like the color screen Palma 2 Pro, the Palma 3 supports the Boox InkSense Plus active stylus so you can use the e-reader as a digital notepad with your preferred note-taking app. But it’s not included. The stylus is an optional upgrade that will add another $46 to the cost of the Palma 3, pushing it closer to the price of premium e-notes like the Remarkable Paper Pure.

title: Nitter and XCancel are dead (again) after X’s latest legal actions
snippet: The privacy-friendly services for viewing X posts without an account have gone dark again after X's escalated legal action.
fullText:
After X threatened legal action last month, Nitter and XCancel, privacy-friendly services for viewing X posts, appear to be officially dead — for real this time. 

Nitter, an open source project that let people read X posts without logging in, had been used to power a number of services, like XCancel and others. But last month, X sent Nitter a cease-and-desist letter over its alleged “unlawful use and circumvention” of X’s API and associated data.

Essentially, X said that Nitter had scraped the social network’s data to access accounts and session tokens in violation of its rules.

Despite the threat, Nitter said on its GitHub page that “following legal advice, the Nitter project will continue,” and promised more details would come soon. In early September, both Nitter and XCancel were up and running again after a short pause.

Unfortunately, things have since changed. 

Nitter’s GitHub page was archived on Friday, September 11, indicating it’s now in read-only status and can no longer be modified or updated. XCancel, meanwhile, shut its service down on Monday, and published a new message on its home page: “Unfortunately, due to a new development in the ongoing legal proceedings, we are required to suspend this service again until further notice.”

Image Credits:XCancel

Nitter, which worked by fetching public X posts and then stripping out the ads, tracking cookies, and JavaScript, gave people a clean, clutter-free way to read posts without an account or the social network’s app.

For X, however, this is not ideal, as it doesn’t want people to access its content without being able to monetize those views with ads. That’s also why Twitter had disallowed third-party apps from accessing its content years ago, wiping out popular services like Twitterrific and Tweetbot along the way.

This wasn’t X’s first attempt to shut down Nitter, but it seems to have worked. Back in 2024, Nitter’s main instance, Nitter.net, temporarily went offline after X rolled out new API restrictions. After that crackdown, those who wanted to host a Nitter instance had to connect it to a real X account.

For lurkers, the services’ closures are a bummer, as they had offered a way to view what was happening on X without having to actually participate on X or help it boost its user numbers. 

Nitter did not respond to a request for comment.

title: AEO startup Profound hits unicorn valuation, raises $180M Series D 7 months after last round
snippet: Profound has raised a $180 million Series D at a $1.8 billion valuation, less than seven months after it raised a $96 million Series C.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

8:22 AM PDT · September 15, 2026

Image Credits:Profound

		

							

											
									

					

	

Profound, which builds marketing software to help brands appear in AI search results, on Tuesday said it has raised a $180 million Series D at a $1.8 billion valuation, less than seven months after it raised a $96 million Series C.

Sequoia and Kleiner Perkins led the round, and existing investors — including Lightspeed Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures, and South Park Commons — also participated. 

Launched two years ago, Profound started as an analytics platform, and has since expanded to help companies research and create marketing strategies. The startup helps businesses understand how AI helps consumers discover their brands. 

It’s part of a wave of startups in the GEO/AEO space (generative engine optimization and answer engine optimization, respectively), where companies try to find ways to surface their products in the AI systems customers are increasingly using for search. 

The company says its revenue has increased by 3x in the past six months, and it now has more than 1,000 enterprise customers, which include Comcast, The Estée Lauder Companies, and Walmart.

title: What if social media isn’t hurting kids?

fullText:
Two years ago, social psychologist Jonathan Haidt released his New York Times bestseller The Anxious Generation. The book posits that the rise of social media and smartphone use is largely to blame for the prominent decline in teen mental health since 2010. It quickly became a central rallying cry of the social media backlash. Haidt has been credited with helping inspire Australia’s nationwide teen social media ban. He has joined forces with bereaved parents who are fighting tech companies in court. His name comes up unprompted in conversations with people in power who say his book opened their eyes to an online crisis.

Haidt’s theory has received regular critiques from recognized academics. Candice Odgers, a leading adolescent mental health researcher, wrote a scathing review of Haidt’s analysis in Nature that opened by conceding, “this book is going to sell a lot of copies, because Jonathan Haidt is telling a scary story about children’s development that many parents are primed to believe.” Now, in the wake of that highly accurate prediction, a former colleague of Haidt’s seeks to not only take down his theory, but also offer an alternative. The biggest question may not be whether he’s correct — but whether it’s too late to change course if he is.

In his new book Restoring Childhood, psychology researcher Peter Gray argues that teens’ mental health declined thanks to decades of steadily reduced autonomy, and after a brief period of reprieve, fell again in the 2010s not — as Haidt argues — because of phones and social media, but because of rigid schooling methods linked to the Common Core curriculum and government pressure to improve children’s performance. And far from being damaging, Gray also argues the adoption of home internet in the 1990s and 2000s actually drove a rebound in teens’ mental health by restoring freedom and connection lost in earlier decades. He fears social media bans aren’t just — as Odgers has argued — a distraction from real solutions, but a new harm in themselves.

“You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy”

In an interview on The Vergecast, Gray told me that Haidt’s book “completely ignored” dozens of meta-analyses and other research that’s found “not even a meaningful correlation between the amount of time kids are on social media or on smartphones and their mental health.” Where there is some connection, Gray adds, studies suggest that teens may use social media to cope with their depression or anxiety. He references a study in Florida that found 11-to-13-year-olds who owned smartphones were more likely to spend real-world time with friends. “You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy and they’ll have less friends,” he says.

Gray says that in studies through the years, kids consistently identify school pressure, not social media, as their top source of anxiety. “That doesn’t mean it’s the primary source for everybody, but when you’re looking at the population at large, every single study that I’ve been able to find where kids are asked, ‘What’s the primary source of your anxiety or your stress or your depression?’, in every single one of them, school pressure comes out on top,” Gray tells me. “Nothing else comes close.”

Gray and Haidt both believe that since at least the 1980s, increased restrictions on kids’ independence and unstructured play have damaged their resilience. While it used to be common for kids to play together unsupervised, that practice has diminished in part due to the rise of “stranger danger” narratives fostered by rare, but high-profile, crimes. In 2017 the pair helped cofound an organization called Let Grow, which advocates for policies that make it easier for parents to let their children play freely, like ensuring they can’t be considered neglectful for letting kids outside by themselves. But the two have split sharply over the impact of the internet. Gray’s book is intended as a deliberate rebuttal to Haidt’s — after The Anxious Generation’s release, Gray resigned from the board of Let Grow to avoid conflict within the organization.

Haidt did not respond to a request for comment from The Verge, but he told The Atlantic’s Kaitlyn Tiffany in a July article that the 1990s and early 2000s dip in teen suicide rates may be credited to a phase-out of leaded gasoline, since lead exposure has been linked to mental health issues. He also told Tiffany that Gray relied too heavily on a minority dissenting group of researchers. Tiffany writes that many of the more than a dozen tech and child development researchers she spoke to “expressed concern that Haidt overstates the strength of correlational findings and suggests causation where it hasn’t been proved.”

Gray accuses Haidt of stirring a moral panic over technology that isn’t, on the whole, harmful. Looking across research, he says, Common Core is the clearest explanation for the sudden decline in teen mental health. And at the population level, the impact of social media “balances out. Some kids are doing better, some kids are doing worse because they’re on social media.”

“We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots”

Gray says he’s not opposed to all guardrails, including school phone bans and the concept of age verification for accessing pornography. But he questions the effectiveness of bans on social media, knowing kids are likely to get around them, and is hesitant to restrict platforms that let kids express themselves — suggesting instead that parents focus on teaching their children to navigate them. “We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots,” he told me. “We need to start understanding that kids are pretty good at knowing what’s good for them and not good for them and they can benefit from our help in learning how to do these things.”

But increasingly, parents of younger teens may not have that choice. Haidt’s theory holds undisputed dominance in many circles, including among politicians. Since Australia’s social media ban for teens, the UK and European Union are among those considering their own bans or platform limits. In the US, states like California and New York have enacted limits on certain social media features, and a federal proposal would restrict algorithmic feeds for kids under 17. Even among people who find Gray’s arguments about Common Core convincing, some might still see taking kids offline as a harmless precaution.

With so much momentum behind the backlash against phones and social media, can Gray’s book still make a difference? “I certainly hope it’s not too late,” he says. He points out that some moral panics have petered out. In the 1990s and 2000s, for instance, many people worried that video games like Mortal Kombat and Doom were making kids more violent, connecting their rise to that of school shootings. Eventually, research showed many mass shooters didn’t play video games after all. Attempts at regulation — including a California ban on the sale of violent games to children — were largely overruled. And many kids who did play them grew up to become those in charge. “The science won out eventually,” Gray says. “So it’s not me that’s going to win out. It’s the science that’s going to win out.”

title: Another Intel iMac has joined Apple’s vintage products list
snippet: After adding three MacBook models to its obsolete products list last month, Apple today updated its vintage products list to include the 2019 21.5-inch iMac with Retina 4K display. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After adding three MacBook models to its obsolete products list last month, Apple today updated its vintage products list to include the 2019 21.5-inch iMac with Retina 4K display. Here are the details.

iMac (Retina 4K, 21.5-inch, 2019) now vintage worldwide

Apple maintains a list of vintage and obsolete products, which lets users know whether older devices are still eligible for hardware service and replacement parts.

The company considers a product vintage once it has been off the market for more than five but less than seven years. Products may become obsolete once Apple has stopped distributing them for more than seven years.

Apple doesn’t necessarily move products to the obsolete list as soon as they cross that threshold, as service and parts availability can vary by product. That said, once a product is classified as obsolete, Apple and its authorized service providers generally stop offering hardware service for it, and parts can no longer be ordered.

Today, the company added the iMac (Retina 4K, 21.5-inch, 2019) to its vintage products list, which means it may still be eligible for hardware service and replacement parts, but they’re subject to availability.

In practice, if you own this iMac and have been putting off a repair, it might be a good idea to get it serviced sooner rather than later.

title: Samsung Gallery is adding Google Photos backup to replace OneDrive
snippet: New updates are starting to roll out that will let Samsung Gallery replace its OneDrive integration with Google Photos support. more…
fullText:
New updates are starting to roll out that will let Samsung Gallery replace its OneDrive integration with Google Photos support.

Earlier this year, Samsung Gallery removed integration with OneDrive and, in turn, also removed native cloud backup for Galaxy users. Users could, of course, use apps from Microsoft, Google, Amazon, or any other number of providers, but there was nothing built into Samsung’s own Gallery app anymore.

Now, Samsung is confirming its replacement.

In an update to the “Gallery Cloud Sync” app on Samsung devices, the company says:

	

Gallery Cloud Sync is a service that safely backs up your precious memories to Google Cloud, allowing you to enjoy them seamlessly on all your devices at any time. View photos taken on your smartphone right away on your tablet.

Easy and secure backup: Safely store your Gallery photos, videos, and albums in the Cloud.

Seamless multi-device sync: No matter which device you use, your Gallery is always kept identical and up to date.

Google Cloud-based reliability: Provides a fast and stable environment through Google’s trusted cloud storage.

Edited for formatting

The mention of “Google Cloud” here is a bit misleading, as Samsung Gallery is adopting direct Google Photos integration, as shown by an early preview of this functionality by @WigettaGaming and SammyGuru writer “That Josh Guy” on Twitter/X. It’s not live just yet – at least in our testing – but Samsung Gallery will offer support for “Sync with Google,” including the ability to see available storage via the Gallery app, choosing which albums to sync, and what data conditions must be met to sync.

Samsung requires the “Gallery Cloud Sync” app and “Samsung Cloud” to both be updated, but it seems a Gallery app update or perhaps even a full system update will be required to get this working fully.

Google Photos integration like this has existed for a few years now, previously being added to the OnePlus Gallery app in 2024 and on devices from Xiaomi and select other brands. Google’s support page on the topic does not yet mention Samsung.

Samsung Gallery will still let existing OneDrive users sync their photos through September 30, but it’s great to see a replacement lined up.

title: SpaceX will try to put Starship in orbit for the first time on September 22
snippet: Elon Musk's company will also attempt to deploy the first V3 Starlink satellites into its orbital internet constellation.
fullText:
SpaceX is ready to perform the 14th test flight of its Starship mega-rocket, and now the company will finally try to put the upper stage into Earth’s orbit for the first time, the company announced Tuesday.

The test launch is scheduled for September 22, with a 75-minute launch window opening at 7:15 a.m. CT. During the test launch, SpaceX plans to deploy the first batch of third-generation Starlinks into its network of 10,000 internet satellites. The company expects to launch 26 V3 satellites into orbit in this test flight. 

If successful, this will be the first Starship launch to generate revenue for SpaceX’s launch division (even if that revenue is coming from another division of the company).

This will be the second Starship test launch since SpaceX became a publicly traded company in the largest IPO in history in June. The first came in July, when SpaceX successfully deployed V3 Starlink satellites for the first time — though those were only meant to test Starship’s deployment capability and burned up in Earth’s atmosphere after roughly 20 minutes.

Getting Starship’s upper stage into orbit around Earth would represent a major milestone for SpaceX. The company has spent billions of dollars on the program and is now looking to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets in favor of Starship. Founder and CEO Elon Musk has said that will happen once Starship is flying “reliably several times per week” to save “scarce SpaceX engineering and production resources.”

SpaceX needs Starship to reliably reach orbit, return to Earth, and get quickly reused to fulfill the massive launch cadence promises that it made during the IPO process.

Starship’s 14th test flight will only test the first part of that equation, though. Musk recently walked back previous claims that SpaceX might try to use its launch tower to catch the Starship upper stage during this flight, saying an explosion would be too big a setback for the company at this point.

SpaceX also won’t try to catch the Super Heavy booster this time. The company has struggled with the booster during its last few test flights and has made multiple changes to try to prevent failures. Yet the booster still struggled to properly relight its engines after separating from the Starship upper stage on Flight 13 in July. For this mission, SpaceX said Tuesday that it made another round of “several modifications” to the booster’s hardware and software to “address issues seen on the previous flight.”

SpaceX had far more success with the upper stage of Starship on Flight 13. While it did not reach orbit, it had a smooth flight through a simulated landing in the Indian Ocean. The upper stage didn’t even explode when it tipped over into the water, allowing SpaceX to spend the last few months capturing and slowly towing it back to its Texas headquarters. 

SpaceX said Tuesday that it has made additional changes to the Starship heat shield based on what it learned from studying the recovered upper stage from Flight 13.

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

		

Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane.

title: Spotify’s newest feature has been on my Apple Music wishlist for years
snippet: Today Spotify announced a feature every parent has probably asked for: the ability to exclude kids and family music from their algorithm. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Today Spotify announced a feature every parent has probably asked for: the ability to exclude kids and family music from their algorithm. Here are the details.

Parents can use new toggle so Spotify Wrapped and recommendations don’t include children’s music

A core feature of modern music streaming services is their ability to recommend music you’ll love.

But if you’re a parent, you know that children’s music has long been a blind spot for Spotify and Apple Music.

I have a toddler, so much of my Apple Music activity these days consists of Mickey Mouse Clubhouse and other children’s songs. Thus, my recommendations and Apple Music Replay are more tailored to my child than me.

But Spotify just launched the solution, and I really hope Apple follows suit soon. Per Spotify:

Starting today, we’re rolling out a new toggle in your settings that lets you exclude kids and family music from your taste profile, so those streams no longer shape your recommendations. This includes, for example, the songs you play on repeat from your kids’ favorite animated movies, theme songs from family TV shows, nursery rhymes, and more.

When you turn this setting off, you can still search for, listen to, and build playlists of kids and family music, but those streams won’t affect what Spotify suggests for you. That means experiences like Discover Weekly, Daily Mix, and Wrapped more accurately reflect your taste. And yes, it applies retroactively, so kids music you’ve already listened to won’t count toward your Wrapped top song or artist, for example.

I’m shocked at how long it took for a feature like this to arrive. But I’m thrilled that it’s finally here.

To use the new toggle, go to ‘Settings and privacy’ in the Spotify app, then ‘Content and display,’ and switch off the toggle labeled ‘Include kids and family music in taste profile.’

If you’re an Apple Music user, one alternative workaround is to use Focus modes to toggle listening history on and off. But I imagine most parents won’t have the mental bandwidth to remember to switch modes back and forth constantly, so it’s not a great solution.

How do you handle streaming children’s music as a parent? Let us know in the comments.

title: Galaxy S26 series reportedly getting a price hike imminently, could be as much as $100
snippet: In the era of RAMageddon, the price hikes just keep coming. Samsung has left its Galaxy S26 untouched thus far, but a new report suggest prices hikes of around $100 could be on the way. more…
fullText:
In the era of RAMageddon, the price hikes just keep coming. Samsung has left its Galaxy S26 untouched thus far, but a new report suggest prices hikes of around $100 could be on the way.

The Galaxy S26 series launched in February with the base S26 and S26+ seeing slight price bumps from their predecessors, and the Ultra unchanged – $899, $1,099, and $1,299, respectively. But a lot has changed in the time since, and it seems Samsung may be bumping those prices further up.

Hans Economy reports that, at least in Korea, Galaxy S26 prices “will be abruptly raised starting October 1.” The planned price hikes (and their converted pricing in USD) follow:

Galaxy S26: 1,254,000 won > 1,403,600 won ($930~ > $1,040)

Galaxy S26+: 1,452,000 won > 1,601,600 won ($1,077~ > $1,188~)

Galaxy S26 Ultra: 1,797,400 won > 1,947,000 won ($1,334~ > $1,444~)

Apparently, Samsung is making this move based on two factors; the continual rise of component costs, and the fact that Apple also just hiked its iPhone prices. The latest iPhone 18 Pro launches are more expensive while the iPhone 17 also saw a $100 price hike in the US (more on 9to5Mac), with the lineup now starting at $899 in the US and 1,450,000 won in South Korea.

	

With that comparison in mind, it’s harder to imagine Samsung plans to bring these price hikes to the US, as they’d make Galaxy flagships $100 more expensive than iPhones across the board, but anything’s possible. 

Samsung, commenting on the report, says that “nothing has been finalized” yet (translated):

We have not sent out any official notice regarding a price increase for the Galaxy S26 series… While it is true that we are internally reviewing whether to adjust prices in consideration of cost burdens, such as the recent rise in component prices, nothing has been finalized as of now.

title: Google Maps rolling out Android Auto speed limits and speedometer that show even without navigation
snippet: While the speedometer has been hit or miss for some Android Auto users as of late, Google Maps is now confirmed to be rolling out speed limits and a speedometer that show at all times, even when you don’t have a destination selected. more…
fullText:
While the speedometer has been hit or miss for some Android Auto users as of late, Google Maps is now confirmed to be rolling out speed limits and a speedometer that show at all times, even when you don’t have a destination selected.

Speed limits in Google Maps launched back in 2019, with the live speedometer appearing later and only starting to show up on Android Auto a few months ago. Earlier this month, though, the speedometer vanished for some users. 

Google is now confirming two things.

First, the disappearing speedometer is being investigated by the Android Auto team. In other words, it appears to be a bug of some kind rather than an intentional removal or rollback of the feature.

	
	

More interesting, though, is that Google is rolling out the ability to see the speed limit of the current road as well as the live speedometer on Maps via Android Auto even when a destination is not set. There have been intermittent reports of this for a few weeks now, but Google is confirming that it’s actually rolling out.

…the ability to have the speedometer, speed limit, and traffic signals/stop signs showing without a destination set is still rolling out. Thus, not everyone will have this particular feature yet.

The exact timeline for when this will be widely available remains to be seen, but it’s great to see nonetheless. Drivers are very often using Google Maps navigation, but shorter or more familiar trips don’t always require setting a destination – but it’s still nice to see speed limits and the speedometer at those times.

title: watchOS 27 now available for Apple Watch, here’s what’s new

fullText:
Apple has released its next major update for Apple Watch users: watchOS 27 is rolling out now. Here’s what’s new.

watchOS 27 adds Siri AI, new Health features, Siri modular face, Tap gesture, and more

Apple Watch users, there’s a major new software release rolling out now. watchOS 27 can be installed via the Watch app on your iPhone, but you’ll need to install iOS 27 first.

watchOS 27 drops support for a large number of previous Watch models. No longer supported are Apple Watch Ultra (1st generation), Apple Watch Series 8, Apple Watch Series 7, Apple Watch Series 6, or Apple Watch SE (2nd generation).

New in watchOS 27 you’ll find:

Two new apps: Siri and a consolidated Find My app

Siri AI, a big upgrade to the assistant that’s far more powerful

Tap gesture for navigating the Smart Stack

Dynamic App Grid as latest default Home Screen view

Siri Modular watch face

New health and fitness upgrades

Design updates

Battery optimization suggestions

Unfortunately, three features have been removed too

Siri AI is clearly the standout change, as the new Siri offers the same powerful assistant that’s found on iPhone in iOS 27 and Mac in macOS Golden Gate.

Rather than implementing a stripped-down version of Siri for the wrist, Apple chose to make watchOS 27’s Siri AI just as capable as on other platforms. And conversations you have with Siri on Apple Watch will sync to all your devices via the new Siri app.

Finally, Apple also says watchOS 27 should run smoother than before thanks to additional bug fixes and refinements that could impact many parts of your everyday experience.

title: tvOS 27 available now for Apple TV 4K, here’s everything new
snippet: tvOS 27 is the latest software update for Apple TV 4K, and it’s rolling out now to all users. Here’s what’s new in tvOS 27. more…
fullText:
tvOS 27 is the latest software update for Apple TV 4K, and it’s rolling out now to all users. Here’s what’s new in tvOS 27.

tvOS 27 adds revamped Apple Podcasts app, new Apple Music features, custom text sizes, more

tvOS 27 is now available to install via the Settings app on your Apple TV. The software is compatible with all Apple TV 4K models except the first generation; Apple TV HD is not supported.

Apple’s new tvOS 27 update adds the following features and changes:

Podcasts: Apple Podcasts gets a revamp on tvOS that follows a similar iOS update earlier this year. The new tvOS Podcasts app fully supports Apple’s new video features, making it a great place to watch video podcasts. And there’s a fresh design with sidebar navigation and more.

Software Updates via iPhone: One convenient tvOS 27 change is that you can now update your Apple TV 4K’s software directly from your iPhone. Using iOS 27’s Home app, you’ll be able to install tvOS 27 and subsequent updates without actually booting up your Apple TV.

Apple Music upgrades: Apple Music gets two new features in tvOS 27. AutoMix is coming to Apple TV as a fresh option for song transitions that are more DJ-like and could fit in well at a party. Hi-Res Lossless Audio is another addition, available for users with compatible external speaker outputs.

Larger text sizes: You can now use Dynamic Type in the Settings app to customize the size of text systemwide, letting you make it larger to better suit your needs and viewing setup.

Finally, Apple says that tvOS 27 supports faster AirPlay connections, smoother animations and app launches, and makes Control Center more responsive.

What’s missing: Siri AI and smart downloads

Notably missing from tvOS 27 is the new Siri AI assistant. Only the old Siri is offered. Rumors indicate that’s because a new Apple TV 4K is about to launch with hardware upgrades that can power Siri AI.

Another missing upgrade is a “Smart downloads” feature that Apple mentioned at WWDC. tvOS has never previously supported downloads for TV content, so it was a surprising announcement. It’s possible “Smart downloads” refers to something system-related and doesn’t involves shows and movies. In any case, there’s been no sign of the feature in the tvOS 27 beta.

title: The Wolverine Game Sinks Its Claws Into Emotional Heights Rather Than Story Cohesion
snippet: A bold foray into an alternate universe crashes Logan against dysfunctional families, doomed love and antimutant violence, but its logic frays as the game goes on.
fullText:
The Marvel superhero Wolverine has been a fan favorite for so long that he’s been spread across a lot of media, splintering his identity as much as his character’s memory: Is he an X-Man, an Avenger, a lone wolf, a team leader, an ancient soldier, a savage berserker, a noble warrior? Insomniac, tapped to make a game centered around the surly mutant who can heal anything except his attitude, opted for a linear adventure hitting the emotional beats of belonging and betrayal — and getting the character’s claws bloody. 

Insomniac was already a beloved studio, with the Spyro, Ratchet and Clank, and Resistance franchises behind it, but its trio of Spider-Man games shot it to another level. There in the bright streets of a sprawling (if abridged) New York City, Insomniac unfurled stories of the web-slinging Peter Parker and Miles Morales that enthralled with polished gameplay and engaging emotional heft. The high-water mark had been reached. How would the studio approach a very different hero, tied not to a villain-ridden city but to causes, themes and time?

In Wolverine (the game), Insomniac abandoned the open world for a chapter-based tale bouncing from locale to locale, narrowing the lens to Wolverine (the character, going by Logan) and a small circle of allies, frenemies and foes. It’s a functional structure to keep the scale personal, though this ends up making a lot of the game feel like a string of room-by-room fights (or chat cutscenes) where the people in Logan’s life flit in and out. It works fine, effectively controlling the pace and narrative to deliver emotional beats, but omitting sidequests and tucking collectibles behind a side door instead of scattering them across a city.

That’s the price to pay for this journey: move forward through Insomniac’s plot beats unfolding along a very straightforward path, fight what’s in front of you, and enjoy the emotional story. If you boil it down to extremes, the one thing setting this game apart from a series of cutscenes is the combat, which pits Logan against anything from handfuls to mobs of enemies who he can skewer and dice apart with attacks and abilities. Though the novelty doesn’t last, combat is initially brutally satisfying, with an escalating rage that grows more vicious, showering Logan in a comical yet worrying volume of blood.

This is one of several ways Logan ends enemies. You’ve been warned.Insomniac Games/Screenshot by CNET

It’s this oscillation between severe violence and emotional interchange that grounds the game in the character of Wolverine, even if the plot’s cohesion frays further into the game. The character beats, backed by honed dialogue, kept me engaged to the end — and while the writing won’t please everyone, its strong start hooked me enough to keep going. Between missions of continuous violence, Logan gets moments of downtime to chat with his allies and fill in the backstory of a game that drops you into a very different world than Wolverine typically inhabits. In this one, the X-Men don’t exist.

This premise is one of the game’s strengths. In the opening scene, a feral Logan, barely a man, growls at the outstretched hand of another whose British accent and elegant suit evoke a familiar scene: the mentor bringing the wildling back to his humanity. But contrary to expectations, this isn’t Charles Xavier. Instead, he introduces himself as Nathaniel Essex. Comics fans know him as Mister Sinister.

Nathaniel Essex, aka X-Men villain Mister Sinister, appears to bring Logan back from his feral bottom of the barrel.

How far you can go with an ‘evil alternate universe’

Without the conventional goodness of the X-Men, evil battles itself. Essex strives for the liberation of mutants like himself, only with brutal methods fronted by Team X, a squad made up of the level-headed Mystique, the violent sociopath Sabretooth and, once upon a time, Wolverine, who left out of a vague frustration with the team’s savage means. Opposing them is human supremacist Bolivar Trask and his private military, who seek to wipe out mutants with his Sentinel hunter-killer robots.

To a comics fan, that’s a neat subversion, prompting the question of who Logan is without the moralizing guidance of Professor X and his X-Men teammates. Anyone else without a decent familiarity with Wolverine’s world likely has a tougher time grasping the significance of this alternate universe. As a member of the former, I enjoyed how this reality created space to decide whether the best-known X-Man has an inborn decency or was always clay in the hands of his rehabilitator. 

As part of Essex’s black ops squad Team X, Logan teams up with Mystique (left) and Sabretooth, who are typically X-Men villains.Insomniac Games/screenshot by CNET

The game’s conclusion won’t shock you, but Insomniac spends good screen time tempting Logan into doing the devil’s work for the right reasons. As a dark mirror of the squabbling but wholesome X-Men, the squabbling and brutal Team X offers Logan a belonging he craves despite his disgust at their methods. Family dysfunction is a strong theme in the game. Love, a little less so.

When hunting down some of Trask’s goons, Logan runs into, and teams up with, a red-headed telekinetic. X-Men fans will pick up on the game’s hints as to her identity — Jean Grey, who in many other versions of the characters, has an unfulfilled romance with Logan owing to her greater commitment to X-Man Scott Summers (Cyclops). Luckily for Logan, he’s nowhere in this game. 

Though they grow closer over the course of the story, Logan and Jean’s attraction is more insisted and fated, within the game and without, than observed. As the lynchpin of a lot of Logan’s later choices, this romance isn’t quite as realized as his messed-up adopted family — but in certain moments that Insomniac takes time to build up, the two pitch a doomed love I couldn’t help but yearn to see fulfilled.

Logan and Jean fall for one another throughout the game.Insomniac Games/screenshot by CNET

Yet plenty of that tension relies on external information. Despite Insomniac’s admirable audacity in making a Wolverine game without the X-Men, plenty of its plot beats and payoffs subvert and evoke character relationships fans know from other media (comics, movies and so on). Players likely won’t care as much about Logan and Jean’s love if they don’t realize it’s the rare What If scenario where Cyclops isn’t standing in the way. 

To get around this, Insomniac makes a radical swerve with Logan’s backstory, tying it into his fractured memory as a late-game reveal that shakily works, so long as you don’t look closely at its timeline or implications. As the studio did with its Spider-Man games, this involves planting seeds for future sequels via references to characters and elements from other corners of classic Wolverine storylines — but these mean nothing to players ignorant of X-Men lore. One of them causes a pivotal consequence for Logan at the very end of the game, and for the uninitiated, it comes out of nowhere. The source of his rage is mired in ambiguity, and even I was perplexed.

The game builds up a handful of big set pieces and bigger bosses.Insomniac Games/screenshot by CNET

As the game’s story heads toward its inevitable conclusion, it never quite answers the nature-versus-nurture question with Logan, and the resolution of his fractured memory frankly isn’t satisfying. Elements from his past are excitedly revealed and never brought up again. Lingering side plots are hastily sewn up as the story barrels toward an abruptly escalated final showdown.

But there’s a core of the game — maybe not the Wolverine I expected, but a Wolverine that Insomniac is clearly invested in exploring — that engages with the character’s relationship between violence and love, belonging and endangerment. I want to play the follow-up that leaves the mystery of Logan’s past behind and carves out a more fulfilling story of changing his destiny with more than just claws.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

David Lumb
						

						

							Managing Editor, Mobile						
					

											

								

											David Lumb is a managing editor for the mobile team, covering mobile and gaming spaces. Before CNET, he covered tech, gaming, and culture for TechRadar, Engadget, Popular Mechanics, NBC Asian America, Increment, Fast Company and others. As a true Californian, he lives for coffee, beaches and burritos.

title: iOS 27 breaks 15 years of muscle memory on iPhone and iPad
snippet: Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order. Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad. iOS 27 is out September 14 after a summer of beta releases. The behavior has changed slightly between the first two releases. However, several developer beta releases later show this change is shipping — even if I’d change it. more…
fullText:
Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is out September 14 after a summer of beta releases. The behavior has changed slightly between the first two releases. However, several developer beta releases later show this change is shipping — even if I’d change it.

Siri AI takes over the swipe gesture for a lot of the iPhone and iPad top edge

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

The last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Notifications now live in the top left corner

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

	

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri. 

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the new behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

iOS 27 is launching Monday, September 14, likely around 10 am PT/1 pm ET.

title: Apple explains how the iPhone 18 Pro’s new Reference Image camera mode works
snippet: A new post on Apple’s Security Research blog details the fascinating tech, architecture, and thinking behind the iPhone 18 Pro’s new Reference Image camera mode. Here are the details more…
fullText:
A new post on Apple’s Security Research blog details the fascinating tech, architecture, and thinking behind the iPhone 18 Pro’s new Reference Image camera mode. Here are the details

Apple explains why it developed the new Reference Image camera mode

In a blog post titled “Apple Reference Image: A New Approach for Verified Photography,” Apple goes in-depth into how its new photographic authenticity system works.

The post confirms that the company’s motivation to build Apple Reference Image was the ever-lowering barrier to creating or adjusting images synthetically.

Apple explains that while industry standards such as C2PA help address the problem, they remain vulnerable to compromise at points in the editing chain.

For this reason, Apple developed a fascinatingly creative chain-of-verification system that is private, secure, and, to the company’s knowledge, “the only image provenance system that provides quantum-secure defenses.”

‘A new standard for verifiable digital photography’

In its explanation, Apple uses classic photography terms, such as a secure digital negative, which contains the raw captured pixels along with information such as signed metadata and timestamps, and is developed in a secure, private, and verifiable environment within the company’s Private Cloud Compute structure.

This semantic authenticity is just one of the three core requirements Apple says a high-assurance photographic provenance system must meet, the other two being resilience to compromise and privacy preservation.

If Apple’s confidence scoring system identifies a sensor as low-scoring and that sensor is revoked, Private Cloud Compute will no longer sign Reference Images captured by it.

Likewise, individual Reference Images can be revoked if later determined to be fraudulent, with Apple devices regularly fetching updated revocation lists.

Another interesting aspect of the Apple Reference Image chain of trust is that it begins once a camera sensor is first initialized, during the iPhone’s manufacturing process.

The sensor generates a signing key pair, keeping the private key to itself while sharing the public verification key with the factory recording station, which then signs it with a factory certificate authority and records it in the device’s hardware manifest.

That private key will later be used to sign every photo taken in Reference Image mode, binding the captured pixel data and sensor metadata to that specific camera sensor before the image ever reaches iOS for further processing.

Apple also uses cryptographic timestamps to establish a verifiable window for when each photo was taken. Instead of relying on a timestamp provided by the device’s general operating system, which the company says can be compromised, the iPhone periodically receives a secure timestamp token that serves as a lower bound.

It then requests another after capture to establish an upper bound, allowing Apple to verify that the image was captured sometime between the two.

The Secure Enclave also plays a role by signing metadata that originates outside the camera sensor. Private Cloud Compute later verifies those signatures, confirms that the sensor and Secure Enclave belong to the same iPhone, and checks the timestamps before developing the secure digital negative.

Once those checks pass, Private Cloud Compute processes the negative into the final JPEG Reference Image and signs it using a combination of traditional and post-quantum cryptography, which Apple says is designed to keep the image verifiable even against future quantum attacks.

Apple goes on to explain that the Reference Image framework was designed so that an outside observer cannot determine the identity of the photographer, which device took a given photo, or whether the same device captured two Reference Images.

This is particularly important, Apple notes, for photographers working in sensitive environments, such as conflict zones, where proving an image is authentic should not require giving up anonymity.

This Security Research blog post makes for a truly fascinating read, even if you are not a technical person. You can read it here.

title: Lukewarm orders for iPhone 18 Pro, says analyst – but it doesn’t mean much
snippet: A high-profile analyst has said that demand for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max appears “lukewarm” based on pre-order wait times. Jeff Pu notes that most iPhone 18 Pro configurations are available for immediate delivery and that the longest wait for the most popular iPhone 18 Pro Max extends only to three to four weeks … more…
fullText:
A high-profile analyst has said that demand for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max appears “lukewarm” based on pre-order wait times.

Jeff Pu notes that most iPhone 18 Pro configurations are available for immediate delivery and that the longest wait for the most popular iPhone 18 Pro Max extends only to three to four weeks … 

Pu says that there’s no delay with most iPhone 18 Pro configs, while availability varies for the Pro Max:

Silver 1TB & 2TB models: Immediate

Black/Glacier 1TB: 1-2 weeks

Burgundy 1TB: 3-4 weeks

256GB and 512GB models in most colors: 3-4 weeks

Assuming consistent supply levels, this would indicate that the iPhone 18 Pro is less popular than most of its predecessors. However, there are so many caveats to this that our take is longer than reporting the data …

9to5Mac’s Take

Actual sales data for Apple products is, of course, extremely commercially sensitive, and the company long stopped revealing unit sales even in earnings reports. There are a number of ways analysts and market intelligence companies can try to get a steer on approximate numbers, however.

The most obvious of these is to look at estimated shipping times for new products. This is a very crude metric as what it actually measures is the gap between supply and demand. A million people wanting a new device and a million devices being stockpiled would still equal immediate delivery, while demand for 100,000 units with only 10,000 in stock would mean lengthy wait times.

Market intelligence companies do use other methods to supplement this. A common one is to use pre-recruited consumer panels who have consented to their inboxes being scanned for order emails. Consumer surveys are also sometimes used. A combination of methods can improve reliability, but ultimately it all amounts to educated guesses.

The huge variable this time around, as Pu himself acknowledges, is that we are still waiting for pre-orders to open for the iPhone Duo. An unknown number of those who would otherwise have ordered one of the iPhone 18 Pro models will be waiting for that instead. “Lukewarm” demand for the iPhone 18 Pro could potentially point to higher than expected demand for the iPhone Duo.

Things will get even more complicated once pre-orders do open for the Duo, since reporting has suggested that production yields have been relatively low, meaning that even modest demand could see lengthy waits for shipping.

title: X and SpaceXAI move to drop Apple from antitrust lawsuit, keep claims against OpenAI
snippet: X and SpaceXAI today filed a motion to voluntarily dismiss their claims against Apple in the antitrust lawsuit they brought against the company and OpenAI. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
X and SpaceXAI today filed a motion to voluntarily dismiss their claims against Apple in the antitrust lawsuit they brought against the company and OpenAI. Here are the details.

Claims against Apple dropped, pending court approval

Last year, Elon Musk accused Apple and OpenAI of colluding to keep competing AI apps from gaining visibility on the App Store.

Soon after, X and xAI (now, SpaceXAI) filed an antitrust lawsuit against both companies, arguing that Apple’s agreement to integrate ChatGPT into Siri and Apple Intelligence gave OpenAI an unfair advantage over rival AI services. Both companies disputed all claims.

Since then, the case has moved into discovery, with the parties fighting over access to internal documents and communications.

A few months ago, a federal judge ordered Musk to turn over potentially relevant emails from his Tesla and SpaceX accounts after OpenAI argued that he had used those accounts to conduct xAI business.

Today, X and SpaceXAI filed a motion to voluntarily dismiss with prejudice their claims against Apple, while keeping their claims against OpenAI.

From the filing:

Plaintiffs have resolved their claims in this Action against Defendant Apple Inc. (“Apple”).

Plaintiffs accordingly move under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a)(2) to dismiss with prejudice their claims against Apple. Apple does not oppose this Motion.

For the avoidance of doubt, Plaintiffs do not seek to dismiss any of their claims against Defendants OpenAl Foundation (f/k/a OpenAl, Inc.); OpenAl, L.L.C.; and OpenAI OpCo, LLC.

Since X and SpaceXAI moved to dismiss with prejudice their claims against Apple, this means that X and SpaceXAI don’t intend to bring those same claims against Apple again in the future. It is worth mentioning that the dismissal is not final yet, as Judge Mark Pittman still needs to approve it.

As for OpenAI, the case now looks somewhat like a spiritual successor to Musk’s separate lawsuit against the company, Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, and Microsoft, which ended earlier this year.

In that case, Musk accused OpenAI of abandoning the nonprofit mission under which it was founded and improperly enriching its executives at his expense. A jury ultimately rejected Musk’s claims in May, finding that they had been filed too late.⁠

title: iOS 27 adds three new iPhone features you’ll use all the time
snippet: iOS 27 launched this week as a major iPhone update, here are three new features that could be among the most-used for many users. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 launched this week as a major iPhone update, here are three new features that could be among the most-used for many users.

#1: Siri AI

Whatever your opinion of Siri has been in the past, iOS 27’s Siri AI is different.

Siri didn’t just get an AI glow-up with a few upgrades. Apple says it “tore [Siri] to the ground” and “rebuilt it from the ground up.”

You can now ask Siri about anything, like you might ask Google or ChatGPT, and it provides informed, helpful answers. It can also perform way more actions on your iPhone than before, and works seamlessly and consistently across all your devices. There’s also a dedicated Siri app to hold all your conversations.

I’ve been using iOS 27’s new Siri for three full months, and it’s became a daily go-to for me.

#2: Automatic proofreading, including for grammar

The iPhone has long offered a basic spellcheck feature that underlines any words it identifies as misspelled. Now in iOS 27, Apple is expanding proofreading in two ways:

spellcheck is now powered by Apple Intelligence  

there’s a new tool for checking grammar

AI being applied to spellcheck means even if a word is technically spelled correctly, you’ll see suggested word replacements if your iPhone thinks the word is being used incorrectly.

Whereas misspellings are typically underlined in red, suggested word replacements and grammar issues are underlined in blue. Compared to common typos, this makes them feel more like optional suggestions rather than in-your-face warning signs.

If you’re not a fan, you can always disable proofreading in Settings. But I’d guess that for lots of users, these features will be welcome iOS 27 additions.

#3: Search overhaul in Spotlight, Photos, and Mail

Search is one of the most essential features for most apps, and certainly for the iPhone as a whole. And in iOS 27, Spotlight search has received a major overhaul.

In addition to having Siri fully integrated with Spotlight, the iPhone’s systemwide search has been rebuilt with a more comprehensive index of your content that always stays up to date throughout the day.

This means you should find Spotlight more useful than ever, as it offers better and more relevant results with every search. Apple says that the same new search foundation powering Spotlight has been implemented in the Photos and Mail apps too, upgrading search across those key apps. title: macOS 27 Golden Gate, macOS Tahoe 26.7, and macOS Sequoia 15.8 fix 200+ vulnerabilities
snippet: If you’re on the fence about installing macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple’s lengthy list of security fixes might be enough to convince you. And if you’re sticking with an older version, you may want to install macOS Tahoe 26.7 or macOS Sequoia 15.8 sooner rather than later. Here’s why. more…
fullText:
If you’re on the fence about installing macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple’s lengthy list of security fixes might be enough to convince you. And if you’re sticking with an older version, you may want to install macOS Tahoe 26.7 or macOS Sequoia 15.8 sooner rather than later. Here’s why.

Apple fixes 200+ macOS vulnerabilities

Apple today published the full security changelogs for macOS 27 Golden Gate, macOS Tahoe 26.7, and macOS Sequoia 15.8, detailing more than 200 vulnerabilities addressed in the updates.

As has been the case with several recent macOS updates, Apple’s acknowledgments include multiple AI-focused security teams and researchers, including OpenAI Codex Security, NVIDIA AI Red Team, and Anthropic Research.

Fixes included in macOS 27 address vulnerabilities that could allow malicious apps or attackers to execute arbitrary code with kernel or root privileges, escape the macOS sandbox, bypass Gatekeeper protections, modify protected system files, access sensitive user data, and more.

One AVEVideoEncoder flaw, for instance, could allow a sandboxed app to execute arbitrary code with kernel privileges. Meanwhile, a UDF file system vulnerability could similarly allow an app to execute code at the kernel level. Apple also fixed vulnerabilities that could lead to remote code execution through Bluetooth, CUPS, and WebDAV.

As for macOS Tahoe 26.7 and macOS Sequoia 15.8, the updates patch many of the same vulnerabilities, including several kernel-level, root-privilege, sandbox-escape, Gatekeeper-bypass, and remote-code-execution flaws listed above.

The older systems also feature some additional fixes not listed for macOS 27, including an ImageIO vulnerability in macOS Sequoia 15.8 that could allow arbitrary code execution when processing a maliciously crafted image.
