title: Google Wallet for Android getting vertically stacked card list
snippet: Following the homepage redesign and fullscreen passes revamp this year, Google Wallet is trialing a vertically stacked card list. more…
fullText:
Following the homepage redesign and fullscreen passes revamp this year, Google Wallet is trialing a vertically stacked card list.

The current design shows your saved credit and debit cards as a carousel at the top of the screen. You swipe horizontally to browse, with this approach showing just a sliver of the next and previous cards at the edges. Google lets you reorder the payment methods and set a default card. This interface allows passes to share the homepage.

The new design uses a vertical list, like the Wallet app on iPhone, that really benefits those with multiple saved cards. Google is showing much more of the card design than Apple, which is a nice aspect of the current look.

This approach is definitely friendlier for one-handed use, especially if your most used cards are placed at the bottom.

	

There are a handful of reports about this rollout over the weekend, with most coming from international users.

GM has been stubbornly standing by its decision to axe Android Auto and Apple CarPlay from many of its newer vehicles in recent years, despite loud and constant negative feedback from consumers. In its latest software update for two new trucks, GM has found the “sweet spot” for implementing Android Auto and CarPlay, but it’s unclear if that compromise will extend to other vehicles. 

A new software experience – based on Android Automotive / Google built-in – debuting in the 2027 Chevrolet Silverado and 2027 GMC Sierra will see GM’s software not only get a nice new coat of paint, but also some welcome functionality. As detailed by CNBC, the update will “proactively surface relevant controls” such as call controls and even a garage door opener. Both vehicles have plenty of physical controls, too.

The biggest news here, though, is GM finding a new way to implement Android Auto and CarPlay integration.

GM announced in 2023 that it would remove phone projection systems from its vehicles while embracing Android Automotive and native functionality in its infotainment system, a decision that has not been positively embraced by customers. While GM has not backed down from this change on its electric vehicles, many of its vehicles still support both platforms. 

	

The change here is that the Silverado and Sierra will support Android Auto and CarPlay, but in a new windowed mode. The projection appears on a part of the display, with aspects of the native infotainment coming through around the sides so you can still easily control parts of the car that projection systems cannot without actually closing anything. 

Speaking to The Verge, GM group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles Colin McCormick explained that this is the “sweet spot.”

I think we’re landing in a spot where… we don’t have a customer that has to decide, “Oh, I’m going to use projection, or, oh, I want to use the native system…” That’s our sweet spot.

That said, there’s no word here on whether or not GM will actually bring Android Auto and CarPlay back to more of its vehicles. Gas-powered vehicles remain with support for phone projection, but that’s still missing in its EVs, including the latest Chevy Bolt that launched earlier this year.

title: This unique retro dock adds a flip-up display, Thunderbolt 5, & 8TB storage to your Mac [Video]
snippet: Amid all the craziness of this iPhone launch week, one of my favorite brands has released its brand-new retro-style dock for the Mac mini and the Mac Studio. Last year, they released their Retro Dock for the M4 Mac mini, and it was the perfect combination of functionality, form, and nostalgia that I had never seen before. It added a ton of ports, an NVMe storage slot, a 5-inch display, all wrapped up in a housing that looked like the original Macintosh from 1984. The new Wokyis G5 & G7 takes it to a whole other level. They’ve added even more pro-level ports, a larger display, usable tactile buttons, while still keeping that retro style look and feel, and they’ve expanded it to both the Mac mini and the Mac Studio. Here is what you need to know. more…
fullText:
Amid all the craziness of this iPhone launch week, one of my favorite brands has released its brand-new retro-style dock for the Mac mini and the Mac Studio. Last year, they released their Retro Dock for the M4 Mac mini, and it was the perfect combination of functionality, form, and nostalgia that I had never seen before. It added a ton of ports, an NVMe storage slot, a 5-inch display, all wrapped up in a housing that looked like the original Macintosh from 1984. The new Wokyis G5 & G7 takes it to a whole other level. They’ve added even more pro-level ports, a larger display, usable tactile buttons, while still keeping that retro style look and feel, and they’ve expanded it to both the Mac mini and the Mac Studio. Here is what you need to know.

Be sure to check out our hands on review where i really showcase how I use the G7 in my worflow. 

The Wokyis G7 Dock

I highly recommend checking out the hands-on video above to get a real sense of how cool and unique this dock’s design is. But when you strip away the look and nostalgia, you still have a high-powered 16-in-1 dock that combines a 7-in display, high-speed connectivity, pro-level ports, physical controls, and an NVMe SSD enclosure. Wokyis offers 10 Gbps and 80 Gbps configurations for the G5 (Mac mini) and the G7 (Mac Studio). I was testing the G7 for the Mac Studio. Some of the key specs you should know are:

7-inch flip-up IPS 1280×800 display

Nine physical and remappable shortcut controls

Thunderbolt 5 connectivity on the 80Gbps model

M.2 NVMe SSD enclosure with support up to 8TB

CFexpress Type B reader rated up to 1,000MB/s

SD & Micro SD 4.0 card reader rated up to 312MB/s

2x USB-C ports with up to 10Gbps speeds

2x USB-A ports with up to 10Gbps speeds

2x additional USB A 2.0 ports

DisplayPort output with support for up to 8K at 60Hz

HDMI port

3.5mm headphone jack

In the box, you also get everything you need. It brings the dock itself, a screw driver for the NVMe enclosure, thermal tape for your SSD, and two braided USB-C 10Gbps cables. One thing to note is that even though this is built to physically fit on top of the Mac mini or Mac Studio, you can use it as a standalone dock with any computer that uses USB-C.

 Thunderbolt 5 is another major feature of the 80 Gbps flagship model. When you connect the dock to your Mac, the 80 Gbps connection enables a supported NVMe SSD to reach speeds that approach internal storage performance. So you no longer need to pay the Apple premium to upgrade your internal storage. Even with SSD storage prices at an all-time high, it is still cheaper to get an NVMe SSD than to upgrade your computer with more internal storage.

But in practice, how well does this all work?

My experience with G7

The first thing that drew me to this dock was the design. The Mac Studio is an incredibly powerful and efficient computer, but the minimal design makes it look like a large, sterile silver box that lacks a bit of personality. Placing the G7 on top completely changes the look and feel of the Mac. This time, Wokyis decided to pull at the heartstrings of retro gamers. The beige finish, directional pad, red action buttons, and flip-up display immediately give the setup a nostalgic gaming aesthetic. Of course, this look is an instant conversation starter to anyone who walks into my office. But after you get over the look, it actually adds a surprising amount of function.

The on-device physical controls actually have a function. They handle actions such as volume adjustments, media playback, copying, pasting, screenshots, screen brightness, and display controls. Then you have the display. At first, I thought it would be more of a gimmick than anything else, but it was surprisingly practical. MacOS recognizes the display just like any other external monitor, so any window or app can be moved over to it, and it instantly scales perfectly. It’s a 7-inch IPS panel with a 1280×800 resolution. I mostly use it for passive data and content viewing. Normally, you will see a video podcast playing when I am getting admin work done, but then, when using it with Final Cut Pro, I use it as a color monitoring system. It works fantastically in that use case. But the use cases are limitless: you can use it for a clock, messages, widgets, system monitoring, and, supposedly, Wokyis is working on a 1st-party utilities app optimized for that display. 

But to me, the most practical benefit is the storage expansion. I use a 4TB NVMe SSD to store all my important files and documents. I use it to run all my FCP projects and even put my apps on it to make sure nothing really sits on my internal storage. And then you have the vast port selection. Personally, I do not use CF Express cards in my workflow, but the fact that it has one is hugely beneficial to others’ workflows. The ports I tend to use the most are the microSD card slot and the 10Gbps USB-C ports. The G7 effectively replaces several accessories that would otherwise be scattered around the desk. 

The G5 version for the Mac mini gives you most of the same, just in a smaller form factor and with a 5-inch display instead of the 7-inch version. The G7 versions will fit on any Mac Studio and the G5 will fit on an M4 Mac mini or newer. And as I mentioned, these will both work with any computer that has a USB-C connection. 

Pricing & availability 

The Wokyis G5 and G7 are available to pre-order on Kickstarter with global shipments starting in October 2026. Pricing for each is:

Wokyis G5 for Mac mini (10Gbps) – $99

Wokyis G5 for Mac mini (80Gbps) – $199

Wokyis G7 for Mac Studio (10Gbps) – $109

Wokyis G5 for Mac mini (80Gbps) – $219

They also offer other bundled options if you want additional accessories. If you are looking for a new USB-C hub for your computer, getting the early-bird special pricing offers great value. The eventual retail pricing will be $369 for the Wokyis G7 80Gbps.

Final take

For me, this comes down to uniqueness and function. Tech is getting more sterile in its appearance because it has become a tool and a utility. These Macs just work so well now because they’re so well integrated with both software and hardware. So the hardware doesn’t need to be flashy. That opens the door to products like the Wokyis G5 and G7. They add a level of character and nostalgia that instantly start a conversation in any environment. But the key here is that it also serves a function; it is not just an empty beige shell. The display is actually very practical and useful. You get all the pro-level ports you need, and it gives me the option to expand my storage. 

So if you are in the market for a new hub for your Mac, or you have a techie in your life who you know would love this, I think the price-to-performance-to-nostalgia factor makes this an easy recommendation.

title: Apple is designing its own game controllers for iPhone, could be Beats branded
snippet: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has today corroborated references discovered in macOS beta code that indicated Apple is designing its own game controllers for iPhone. Apple already sells some controllers like the Backbone One (pictured above) and SteelSeries Nimbus+ through the Apple Store, and now it wants to take a slice of the iPhone gamepad market for itself. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has today corroborated references discovered in macOS beta code that indicated Apple is designing its own game controllers for iPhone. 

Apple already sells some controllers like the Backbone One (pictured above) and SteelSeries Nimbus+ through the Apple Store, and now it wants to take a slice of the iPhone gamepad market for itself. 

The code findings indicated the development of two controllers, with model identifiers T6502 and T1057 respectively. The code findings showed evidence of a D-Pad, thumbsticks, haptic motors, and possibly an integrated accelerometer and gyroscope for motion controls. However, the exact design of what the Apple-made game controllers look like is not yet known. 

Gurman believes the Apple-developed accessory may ultimately be released under the Beats brand, with the project being overseen by Beats executives. Beats accessories often target lower price points with slightly cheaper materials than the more premium Apple brand implies. 

As a reminder, users can connect MFI-compatible game controllers to their Apple devices, as well as traditional game console controllers like the PlayStation DualShock and the Xbox Wireless Controller. 

An Apple or Beats-branded game controller could also help improve the gaming ecosystem on Apple TV 4K, and boost engagement with the increasingly-sophisticated AAA games being made available on iOS and Mac.

title: Google’s hyper-personalized ‘Dreambeans’ feed is now free to test [U]
snippet: Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test. more…
fullText:
Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test.

Update 9/10: Google officially announced the broader availability today.

Personalized topics: This could be everything from places to explore, shows to watch, or a reminder of upcoming events.

Connected apps: Distilled information from the Google apps you select, including Calendar, Gmail, Photos, Search, YouTube, and now Gemini.

Original 8/28: Dreambeans is very much like a hyper-personalized Google Now or Discover feed. Like the Gemini app and AI Mode, it uses Google’s Personal Intelligence system to learn your interests by looking at your Gmail, Google Photos, Calendar, Workspace, Search history, and YouTube. During setup, you can choose which apps Dreambeans can access.

Workspace supplies ground-truth transaction data like receipts and upcoming flights

Photos provides the visual memories and insights about you and the people in your life

YouTube identifies your active hobbies

Search detects your budding interests

By combining all these unique signals, Dreambeans can proactively generate rich and highly customized daily visual stories.

The app suggests topics to explore, things to try, places to visit, and interesting events. New stories arrive every morning.

	

Instead of using stock imagery, each Dreambeans story is accompanied by Nano Banana 2-generated artwork that uses an illustrated style. For example, if Dreambeans recommends a hike, you might see yourself and a group of friends at that location.

Tapping on a story lets you see a longer description. In the same example, you’ll get trail details, specific places to stop, what to wear, and timing recommendations. Dreambeans will link to trail guide content on the web. There’s also an “Ask anything” chat experience to get more information.

You can leave feedback by tapping the heart or downvoting, while the chat interface allows you to provide more details. “Tune your feed” lets you tell Dreambeans what you “want more stories about” and what it should never show.

The name combines two ideas at the heart of the app. The “dream” is how the app works overnight to find meaning in the content overload across your connected apps. It then distills what it finds into “beans” – a fresh collection of stories brewed for you each morning.

In June, it was just available for Google AI Ultra subscribers, with Google expanding to AI Pro earlier this month. The setup process “requires up to a day to build your first set of stories.” 

It remains to be seen how Dreambeans will graduate from Google Labs. The experience it offers today is largely standalone, with Daily Brief in the Gemini app possibly benefiting from a more visual experience. 

Dreambeans is available on Android and iOS in the US.

title: What an Ex-Anthropic Researcher’s Warning About Human Extinction Really Means
snippet: AI companies think their creations could kill us all. They’re carrying on anyway.
fullText:
A viral series of posts on X from an AI researcher who resigned from Anthropic over ethical concerns has sparked thousands of responses and reignited debate over the potential future dangers of artificial intelligence.

Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who also worked at OpenAI on pretraining AI models, quit his job at Anthropic over concerns that AI development could lead to human extinction. 

“Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Superintelligence refers to a hypothetical scenario in which AI’s “cognitive” abilities vastly exceed those of humans across every domain — science, math, strategy, creativity and problem-solving.

The threaded post on X from Coxon has more than 156 million views as of this writing and has been liked more than 752,000 times.

I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below.

— Jacob Coxon (@hilbertspaess) September 9, 2026

The statement quickly spread on social media and was featured on major news sites. It even drew a comment from Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who responded on X, “It’s becoming more clear the threat AI poses to humanity, so I’m calling for immediate action from the industry and Washington.”

In less than 24 hours, the statement also drew responses from others at Anthropic who, rather than debating with Coxon, confirmed that the threat that AI will overtake and potentially eliminate humans is not a wild fantasy but a reality for AI researchers.

“Jacob [Coxon] is correct here,” wrote Evan Hubinger, a team leader at Anthropic in AI alignment stress testing, on X. Hubinger wrote in his response, “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.”

Hubinger said, “I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”

Representatives for Anthropic and OpenAI didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Resignations that act as warning signs

It’s difficult to dismiss Coxon’s concerns for one big reason: He’s not the first researcher at a major AI company to leave for these reasons. In February, a safety lead at Anthropic, Mrinank Sharma, resigned from the company, telling followers on X, “The world is in peril … We appear to be approaching a threshold where our wisdom must grow in equal measure to our capacity to affect the world, lest we face the consequences.”

In the same month, OpenAI researcher Zoë Hitzig wrote in a New York Times column that she quit the company in part because it was following Meta’s path of prioritizing profits over ethics. Days later, she reposted a poem she’d written on X, titled “How We Programmed the Apocalypse.”

Since then, AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have walked back some of their previous comments about AI’s potential for harm or whether it will create mass unemployment. Anthropic publicly acknowledged earlier this year that it has loosened some of its safety standards to keep up with competitors, including OpenAI and a swath of Chinese companies that have been releasing cheaper, high-performing AI models.

That competition, with both OpenAI and Anthropic hurtling toward initial public offerings, has raised concerns that, instead of moving cautiously in deploying AI models, industry leaders are rushing into the unknown and releasing models that could pose present and future dangers. This was the case when Anthropic released advanced AI models, which ended up being pulled or temporarily restricted due to major cybersecurity risks.

In the case of Coxon, whose resignation has caused the largest stir yet among those who’ve left AI companies, the dangers of contributing to the technology’s accelerating pace outweighed any financial gains. “I left before any of my equity vested,” he told the news site Axios.

Ironically, both OpenAI and Anthropic have taken the stance that if they slow down, someone less concerned with safety will drive AI’s future.

“Coxon is right that competition is driving the speed,” said Shama Hyder, a professor of AI at Link School of Business. “Every one of these companies believes slowing down hands the lead to someone less careful, so even the people who understand the risk have a reason to accelerate. “

AGI and superhuman AI 

How quickly AI poses an imminent threat to humanity may depend on when the technology reaches two purported benchmarks that have become increasingly blurred: superhuman AI (also known as artificial superintelligence or ASI), which Coxon mentioned in his viral post, and AGI, or artificial general intelligence.

AGI would mark the hypothetical point at which AI meets or exceeds the capabilities of a human mind. Some predict that AI will achieve that benchmark in just a few years, or at least sometime before the end of the 21st century. That timeline has also been thrown into doubt by some AI leaders, such as Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who downplayed the importance of such markers on a recent earnings call where he said, “For many tasks, we could say that we have already achieved AGI.” The milestones, he said, “are kind of senseless at this point.”

The goalposts are also varied. Some may choose to measure AGI using specific tests, while others would consider AGI achieved only if AI could act autonomously in ways that surpass human capabilities.

ASI would be further down the road, after AGI, and would theoretically mark the point at which AI could outperform all humans across all tasks, particularly in deep thinking and cognitive understanding. The timeline for that is much fuzzier, but the speed at which AI is advancing has researchers such as Coxon suggesting it’s sooner than many people think.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (left) and US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (right) on stage at the G20 forum this month. Altman has acknowledged the risks of AI while trying to sway the public on the technology’s benefits.Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

A recent event that may have some adjusting their timeframes is the incident exposed in July in which OpenAI agents went rogue, plotted together and hacked Hugging Face, an AI community that Nvidia acquired. The speed at which the Hugging Face incident unfolded and the likelihood that it could happen again — this time without warning — have fueled concerns about the dangers of autonomous AI systems.

Doomers vs. boosters

The debate over whether AI will kill all humans by 2030 mirrors the broader discussion over AI doomers versus boosters, and the lack of nuance in the middle. While AI boosters typically hype AI by emphasizing its extraordinary potential, such as huge productivity gains, AI doomers hype it in the opposite direction, emphasizing job loss and human extinction.

As Emily Bender and Alex Hanna argue in their book The AI Con, both AI boosters and doomers rely on science-fiction tropes to frame superintelligence as either a utopian savior or an apocalyptic threat, despite a lack of evidence that such technology is near. Many AI critics argue that either narrative functions as corporate marketing, with the same underlying premise, falsely presenting an all-powerful AI future as an absolute inevitability.

The speed at which Coxon’s post went viral and the response it’s drawing may be an indication that the AI industry has another PR crisis on its hands in a year when AI data centers are under fire and trying to change their image, and social media companies, including Meta, are reeling from multibillion-dollar judgments over issues like tech addiction.

One approach that AI leaders like Altman have taken is to focus the public’s attention on what AI brings to the table and what it could offer beyond job losses and mass death — in other words, swapping doomer rhetoric for booster rhetoric.

“Abundance” has been a buzzword that’s been thrown around of late, promising a world in which AI’s advances and benefits will eliminate scarcity and improve life for everybody by lowering barriers to creating new goods and services and providing them more cheaply, and not just for those who can afford the costs of advanced AI technology.

Hyder said that what was missing from Coxon’s post was guidance on what people outside the AI industry can do. 

“The extinction debate belongs to a few hundred people who control training runs and the regulators who can inspect them,” she said.

The question ultimately boils down to what humans want to do with the technology. 

“If AI is powerful enough to do the dramatic things people fear, it’s powerful enough to do the dramatic things we’ve been hoping for in medicine and science,” Hyder said.

So far, the hyped-up abundance argument has been met with skepticism, especially when it keeps public attention and fascination focused on AI. Boosterism benefits the companies that are guzzling investment dollars and promoting the billions (or trillions) their companies’ IPOs may represent.

Who cares about abundance, you could argue, if there are no humans left in the world to enjoy it?

title: Google Search kicks off the NFL season with Live Game Feeds and fantasy football advice
snippet: Tonight’s game between the New England Patriots and the Seattle Seahawks isn’t just a Super Bowl LX rematch — it’s also the official start of the 2026 NFL season. Google has invested pretty heavily in football over the past few years through YouTube TV, but today, it’s giving Search some big improvements to make following the season a little easier. more…
fullText:
Tonight’s game between the New England Patriots and the Seattle Seahawks isn’t just a Super Bowl LX rematch — it’s also the official start of the 2026 NFL season. Google has invested pretty heavily in football over the past few years through YouTube TV, but today, it’s giving Search some big improvements to make following the season a little easier.

Google is adding a Live Game Feed to search, which allows fans and spectators alike to follow along with game developments as they unfold on the field. Any active game will show a “Live” icon in search, and selecting that option shows a recap of what’s happened so far alongside a “dynamic timeline featuring play-by-play updates, top social commentary, key video highlights, and AI-powered insights.” This sounds quite a bit like Google’s alternative to something like Apple’s (truly excellent) sports app, though we’ll have to see how it performs in action first.

fullText:
Good morning, how did you sleep? Me, I had trouble until I started counting the number of times Apple used the word “AI” in its keynote (it was 41). In my dream, I was inundated with Elizabeth Holmes deepfakes and memes, which startled me awake. As I lay in bed, I calmed down by reading about how AI will “kill us all by the end of the decade,” and then I got up and helped ChatGPT do my kids’ homework. Such a great day.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column.

⭐️ Starred

Today’s main story is, of course, Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event, which debuted two new iPhone 18 Pros, two new Apple Watches, an updated pair of AirPods at a lower price, and a foldable called the iPhone Duo.

	

As predicted (and pre-empted), the iPhone Duo is a book-style foldable slightly wider and shorter than the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. Apple uses a combination of flexible plastic and thin layers of titanium sandwiched between the OLED panel, and claims that the crease is basically undetectable, though we’ll have to see how well that claim holds up over time. Curiously, Apple has also resurrected the under-display camera, which was a mainstay of Samsung’s Fold line until it disappeared in the Fold 7, as well as Apple Pencil support, which Samsung also dropped in the same generation.

To the credit of Samsung, Oppo, Honor, and even Google, the iPhone Duo does not appear to be dramatically superior to the latest book-style foldables; it matches the latest Pixel Folds’ IP68 water and dust resistance rating (that degrades over time); it relies on a side-mounted fingerprint sensor for authentication over the more convenient Face ID; it only has two cameras, and they lack the upgraded features of the Pro models; and at 254 grams, it’s heavier than practically any other foldable out there today.

What I find more compelling than the hardware is how Apple designed iOS to ostensibly work better with a foldable. Watching the demos, you can immediately see the care that went into the transitions between main and internal displays, and the changes that make the software easier to use with one hand. And while older apps may look funky until they’re updated, Apple has traditionally had better luck than Google convincing (or forcing) developers to adapt their apps to new form factors.

With iOS 27.1, which will be released alongside the iPhone Duo in October, developers will be able to target the foldable in app updates. Apple is banking on the fact that this larger canvas will tempt developers with new ways to earn money, a flywheel that has rewarded the company handsomely over the past 18 years. And hopefully the new attention paid to Apple’s entry will push reluctant developers to consider doing the same for their Android apps — though I’m not holding my breath. 

More from 9to5Mac: Hands-on with the foldable iPhone Duo

✉️ Inbox

Hands-on: Honor’s Robot Phone is probably the coolest phone you still can’t buy. Straight from the IFA floor, Andrew goes hands-on with the most bizarre phone of 2026.

Xiaomi 18 Fold goes on sale with full specs and a Galaxy Z Fold 8 comparison. Xiaomi timed its iPhone Duo competitor perfectly or poorly depending on how you look at it. The phone is intriguing in its own right, with Xiaomi’s first home-grown SoC and a huge 200MP main camera.

Xiaomi Pad 9 Pro Max has a 13.3-inch display, Android 17, and a 12,000 mAh battery

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max melds a classic ARRI camera with an iPhone-like look, launches this month

Samsung’s Privacy Display and TriFold merge in the Huawei Mate XT2. Samsung may have abandoned the tri-fold category, so Huawei is just stealing its best ideas.

Oppo confirms Find X10 Pro Max and its triple 200MP camera setup will launch this month. Another big release for massive cameras, the Find X10 Pro Max follows the ridiculously well-endowed Find X9 Ultra, which our Ben Schoon called “simply stunning” in his review.

Two Galaxy S27 models will get Samsung’s Privacy Display, not just the Ultra. We’re still doing this, huh?

Hands-on: Orbitkey elevated its time-tested key organizer with a built-in Google Find Hub tracker. As someone who loses his keys all the time, this product just makes sense.

Pebblebee’s latest Android Find Hub trackers have bright neon colors, available today

Google Find Hub update brings new ‘Remembered’ tab with Gemini

Boox Picco is exceptionally tiny for an e-reader, but it parts ways with Android and third-party apps. I am an avowed fan of tiny e-readers, and I am also a Boox Palma 2 owner, so I’ll definitely be picking this up when it debuts in November.

Arm’s new CPU cores and GPUs for Android chips promise ‘desktop-class’ games, more AI power. This is the part where I joke about how excited I am to play a ray-traced version of Candy Crush or something, but Arm genuinely knocked it out of the park with this release.

Google Find Hub update brings new ‘Remembered’ tab with Gemini. I cannot wait to abuse the heck out of this feature.

Google Messages rolls out Keep Notes integration on Android. 

Google Search kicks off the NFL season with Live Game Feeds and fantasy football advice. Go Bills!

Today in bugs, bug fixes, and shutdowns:

Google Maps speedometer disappears on Android Auto for some, traffic data still missing too

Google Messages slowly rolling out fix for bug that randomly sends old texts to other people

Samsung is shutting down ‘Quick Measure’ and ‘AR Doodle’ apps for Galaxy phones

Google Pixel Tablet has been discontinued, out of stock everywhere

🍎 Etc.

Apple didn’t just introduce a foldable iPhone yesterday. There was also the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and the AirPods 5.

With the Duo stealing much of the spotlight, it may be easy to overlook the other products, but it’s worth sticking with them for a minute. The iPhones, for instance, feature an upgraded main sensor with a variable aperture, a spec that Samsung adopted with the Galaxy S9 and abandoned two years later. Apple’s implementation offers four stops of range (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0), which are cycled through automatically depending on the environment. I’m not sure how much real-world impact it will have, but the technology has likely come a long way in the past few years, so I’m cautiously optimistic.

Perhaps more interesting is that the iPhone 18 Pro is the first in Apple’s flagship lineup to do away with Qualcomm modems, a change seven years in the making. The C2, which is also in the Duo, is Apple’s first chip to support mmWave in the US, which is required for Verizon’s network. (Oddly, the iPhone 18 Pro Max retains its Qualcomm modem, perhaps because it performs better and can fit into the larger housing.)

The new Apple Watch’s most notable feature may be its most controversial: inside its overarching Audio Intelligence announcement are two features, Live Rewind and Siri Recap, that create transcriptions or summaries of recent interactions. While Apple is quick to point out that no audio data is uploaded to its servers, nor stored permanently on the watch, the reality is that this feature enables surreptitious recording of everyday conversations without consent.

The AirPods 5 is low-key interesting, not because of any particular upgrade but because it’s the only product in Apple’s entire lineup that received a price drop.

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

Watch me and Will Sattelberg talk endlessly about the insane You Can See Everything trailer before dovetailing into a conversation about repairable tech with Fairphone CTO, Chandler Hatton. 

Afterwards, if you still have any brain cells left, you should watch this Metroid Ravenous trailer, which I’ve already seen half a dozen times, and then spend some time with Playdate Season 3, which drops in October.

🎙️ Quotations

I asked the 9to5Google editors to sum up their thoughts on yesterday’s Apple event.

This event really cemented Apple as just another player in the industry, if it wasn’t already. A Pro-tier iPhone leaning on AI tricks as the bulk of its pitch? A foldable that pulls from nearly a decade’s worth of other companies’ devices without bringing much new to the table? What was even new on the Watch Series 12 besides that awful new brown color? Whatever spark of creativity Apple once carried — even from an Android user’s perspective — has been long gone for a while now, but this is the first event where I really felt a burning sense of boredom in the pit of my stomach.

– Will Sattelberg, Senior Writer and Podcaster

The iPhone Duo was the highlight for me; Apple’s entrance to the foldable market was inevitable, and it was fairly well done.

I’m wary of things like the side-oriented UI changes to iOS and the glossy dot in the middle of a matte inner display, but Apple’s usual level of polish has me intrigued. Not enough to drop $2,000 on a device that runs an OS I absolutely loathe, though, especially seeing as Apple didn’t show off much that actually changes the game in terms of using a foldable. The most revolutionary addition was that neat animation when transitioning between displays. For now, I’m still loving my Fold 8.

– Ben Schoon, Senior Editor

Apple did in fact “just walk in” and possibly figure out foldables. That or the reality distortion field was upgraded.

Anyway, I’m personally interested in the Apple Pencil support for the iPhone Duo, while I’m very eager to see how the new sidebar that incorporates status bar icons and the dock feels on the Duo’s cover screen. Ignoring third-party launchers that you have to install yourself, this might be the biggest change in smartphone UX for a bit.

– Abner Li, Editor-in-Chief

No matter how you feel about the iPhone Duo as a device, it’s finally good to see competition begin to heat up for phones that function beyond the range of the smartphones we’ve been using for the over a decade. Unfortunately, that competition is also expensive, just like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 series and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Not entirely unexpected, but a nudging reminder of where technology’s economy is right now. I, for one, am excited to see how the iPhone Duo works in the same tests we throw Android foldables through. If the Duo UX looks as good as Apple’s pre-recorded event makes it out to be, there might be plenty to look forward to for both Apple and Android. And who knows, maybe the iPhone Duo 2 won’t be nearly $2,000.

– Andrew Romero, Senior Editor

After seeing the Duo in the hands of the public, it seems like Apple isn’t magically reinventing the foldable after all.

Apple’s take on foldable software is fun, with lots of good hardware choices that will hopefully positively influence Android foldables. But overall, it hasn’t addressed any huge problems that existing foldables aren’t already dealing with.

– Jordan Floyd, Video Producer

title: Apple Car Keys reportedly coming to three more automakers
snippet: Apple is reportedly preparing to extend Car Key support in Apple Wallet to three more automakers. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple is reportedly preparing to extend Car Key support in Apple Wallet to three more automakers. Here are the details.

Apple adds more automakers to its Car Key backend

As spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple has added three new automakers to its backend code for Apple Car Key: Lincoln, Freelander, and Lucid.

This does not mean, however, that support will be available right away. Backend changes are usually a good indication of upcoming Car Key integrations, but there is nothing in the code pointing to when they will actually launch. Apple has also yet to confirm which specific vehicles will support the feature⁠.

Today’s discovery follows a string of similar backend changes pointing to upcoming Car Key support from other automakers. In July, similar backend references appeared for GWM’s Tank vehicles, followed shortly after by Haval, another brand owned by the same Chinese automaker.

Apple had also previously announced that Lucid would adopt Car Key, alongside a list of brands that included Acura, Cadillac, Chevrolet, GMC, Porsche, Rivian, and others.

Announced at WWDC 2020, Apple Car Key allows drivers to use an iPhone or Apple Watch to lock, unlock, and start a compatible vehicle, with support varying by automaker and model.

It currently works with more than 50 vehicle models from brands including BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Hyundai, Kia, Genesis, Toyota, and Rivian.

title: watchOS 27: Siri app lets you continue existing chats, though it’s a bit hidden
snippet: Apple Watch includes an all-new Siri app in watchOS 27. Unlike the iPhone and iPad versions, it’s a bit less intuitive to use in one way. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch includes an all-new Siri app in watchOS 27. Unlike the iPhone and iPad versions, it’s a bit less intuitive to use in one way.

Siri app comes to iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch

Starting with Apple’s OS 27 software updates, Siri can save chat history for the first time.

This is useful for two reasons. First, you can easily reference something you looked up before without asking again. Second, you can actually resume a conversation with Siri without starting over from scratch. 

Having context in the chat thread changes how you need to communicate with Siri. Suddenly, you’re able to speak more naturally without explaining exactly what you mean each time. It’s a bit like sticking with one customer support agent instead of jumping around a phone tree.

Anyway, Siri apps for iPhone, iPad, and Mac make picking up the conversation intuitive and easy. It’s basically like using an iMessage chat thread.

Meanwhile, on the Apple Watch, it’s fair to determine that the Siri app just doesn’t support resuming chats. The chat threads are displayed, but there’s no obvious user interface for continuing the conversation from within the Siri app on Apple Watch.

How to continue Siri chats on Apple Watch 

Fortunately, there’s a way. The trick? Invoking Siri while the chat thread is open in the Siri app. This can be by holding the Digital Crown or by saying Siri/Hey Siri.

Again, it’s not really intuitive, but it works. Siri on watchOS will append whatever your input is to the chat thread in view. 

There’s probably a better way to do this that we’ll see in a future version of watchOS 27. For now, give it a shot.

watchOS 27 is officially available alongside iOS 27. Siri AI requires specific hardware, supported markets, and may be waitlisted before becoming available. 

Apple Watch Series 12 is currently available for pre-order from $399. Apple Watch Ultra 4 is available for pre-order from $799. Both models launch in one week on September 18.

title: iOS 27.1 release date: Here’s when to expect the new iPhone update
snippet: iOS 27 launches for all users next week, and will be followed not long after by the first iOS 27.1 beta and public launch. Here’s when to expect iOS 27.1’s arrival. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 launches for all users next week, and will be followed not long after by the first iOS 27.1 beta and public launch. Here’s when to expect iOS 27.1’s arrival.

iOS 27.1 launches in October before iPhone Duo release, with beta in the next week or so

If you’re not running Apple’s beta already, there’s a huge iPhone software update coming next week.

iOS 27 launches this Monday, September 14 and is packed with new features like Siri AI.

But if you’ve been running the iOS 27 beta all summer, you’re likely already looking ahead to iOS 27.1.

Apple is expected to debut the first iOS 27.1 beta within about a week of iOS 27 launching. Here’s what we’ve seen in recent years:

iOS 26.1 beta released 7 days after iOS 26

iOS 17.1 beta released 9 days after iOS 17

iOS 16.1 beta released 2 days after iOS 16

I excluded iOS 18 because Apple launched its 18.1 beta extra early during the summer as a way to test Apple Intelligence.

So the typical pattern points to iOS 27.1 beta 1 arriving as early as next week, or as late as the week of September 21.

What about the public launch?

Apple confirmed this week that iOS 27.1 will ship by October 23—and likely a few days earlier.

Its iPhone Duo press release says, “iPhone Duo will be available with iOS 27.1.” Since iPhone Duo arrives in users’ hands on October 23, the software update must be released by then.

This will actually be slightly earlier than we’d normally expect. Starting with 2025, in the last four years Apple’s x.1 updates launched on: November 3, October 28, October 25, and October 24.

Based on iOS 27.1 shipping with iPhone Duo, the most likely public release date for the software is anywhere from Monday, October 19 to Wednesday, October 21.

It’s unknown what all will be included in the update other than iPhone Duo-exclusive changes. But we’ll keep you posted after the first beta arrives.

title: iOS 27 adds new Phone app feature that’s an instant favorite
snippet: iOS 27 is packed with new features for apps like Notes, Wallet, Maps, Messages, and more. But one iOS 27 addition that’s especially impressed me is a new Phone feature: Call Context. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is packed with new features for apps like Notes, Wallet, Maps, Messages, and more. But one iOS 27 addition that’s especially impressed me is a new Phone feature: Call Context.

iOS 27’s Call Context feature puts key info on-screen when you’re on the phone with a business

I’m not a big fan of phone calls, so the Phone app isn’t somewhere I spend much time. But last year in iOS 26, the app had two of my favorite new features: Call Screening and Hold Assist.

Now with iOS 27 this year, Apple has again impressed me with a new Phone app feature.

Call Context is an Apple Intelligence feature that automatically surfaces relevant info on the call screen when you’re on the phone with a business.

Per Apple’s website:

Get relevant information while on a call. Call Context can proactively surface relevant information from across your apps when calling a business — like a confirmation code from Mail when you call an airline.

I’ve had the chance to use Call Context a couple times during the iOS 27 beta. And I’ve very quickly concluded that this is the kind of no-brainer addition that should prove popular.

Recently I booked flights with Southwest Airlines, and later needed to call them about a change. 

When I called, my flight info was automatically put on the screen. My iPhone even offered to read the confirmation number out loud for me on the call.

title: Kia’s electric van lineup is getting more interesting with reveal of PV7
snippet: You may not know it, but minivans are making a comeback in the US. Look around, and you'll start to notice an uptick in these breadboxes on wheels. fullText:
You may not know it, but minivans are making a comeback in the US. Look around, and you’ll start to notice an uptick in these breadboxes on wheels. Sales were up 21 percent in 2025, suggesting that the humble minivan is shaking off its “uncool” stigma and finding new fans among an SUV-weary public. I’m here for it.

One of the companies currently carrying the torch for minivans is Kia, which has sold its popular Carnival minivan here since 2021. Kia is also one of the few automakers making all-electric vans. This week, the Korean automaker rolled out its new PV7 at IAA Transportation in Germany. This is the second electric van from Kia’s Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) lineup, following the PV5 “people mover,” which went on sale in 2025. The PV7 is longer than the PV5 by about 2 feet and comes in two variants, one for passengers and one for cargo.

All of which is to say that Kia should bring its increasingly interesting electric vans to the US. If they are attractively priced — and this is Kia, so it’s safe to assume that’s possible — I really think these vans would do numbers. The people yearn for a moderately priced electric van!

1/5

The PBV vans are technically impressive on several levels. They’re built on Kia’s dedicated PBV architecture (E-GMP.S) that features a flat-floor layout for easy loading and unloading. The PV7 will come with a 71.5kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt battery pack or a 96.2kWh one. Kia claims the Cargo Long-Range version will get 460km (285.8 miles) on the generous WLTP cycle (which tends to be around 10–20 percent more generous than the EPA’s estimates). It’s built on an 800-volt architecture, which enables 10—80 percent charging in under 25 minutes using a 350kW DC fast charger. And it supports vehicle-to-load outlets to power external tools and equipment. The infotainment runs on Kia’s Android Automotive-based Pleos Connect OS, which includes its Gleo AI natural-language voice controls.

1/6

This all sounds great! And the design is just forward-looking enough to erase any concerns about the typical clunkiness of van ownership. The front end features a distinctive two-tone design with a dark upper section that wraps around the windshield, giving it a visor-like appearance. The upright look and tall, flat roof suggests a large interior space perfect for vanlife compartmentalization. The low front bumper and plastic body cladding around the base add a rugged, practical border. Both the passenger and cargo versions feature distinctive wheels with a squarish multi-spoke design. It’s not boring, but it’s not so in your face as to challenge your worldview.

While Kia’s not saying whether the PV7 will be making its way to the US anytime soon, a version has been spotted testing in the US, according to Electrek. Officially, the van will be launched in Europe and Korea in the second half of 2027, with “additional markets, derivatives and conversion models to follow.”

PBV was introduced during CES 2024 as a family of EVs built on a flexible vehicle architecture with different swappable body types. The vehicle can be transformed from a minivan to a full-size van to a small truck, depending on the specific need. The driver cab remains fixed, while the rest of the vehicle is interchangeable, like a real-life Duplo set. Of course, that was a concept from a different era. We’ve now veered into a darker timeline, at least for EVs.

I get why Kia would hesitate to name the US as a future market, what with our well-documented history of cutting off our nose to spite our face. The minivan market may not be as red-hot as, say, the one for lifted trucks that roll coal and grind up spandex-wearing cyclists for breakfast. But the times, they are a-changing. Gas prices are going up and up. And an electric van could just be thing that finally heals our broken nation.

Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

Andrew J. Hawkins

title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs Series 11: Here’s everything new
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 improves many of the core components that power watchOS and the device’s health and fitness features, plus unlocks new AI capabilities. Here’s everything new in Apple Watch Series 12 vs Series 11. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 improves many of the core components that power watchOS and the device’s health and fitness features, plus unlocks new AI capabilities. Here’s everything new in Apple Watch Series 12 vs Series 11.

Design and durability: New case options, Ceramic Shield 2, more

Apple Watch Series 12 comes in the same 42mm and 46mm options as before, but with some design and durability updates.

In terms of case options, Apple Watch Series 12 debuts a new Dark Bronze aluminum finish and also introduces Ceramic, which is available in Pearl White and Night Blue.

Aluminum models of Series 12 add Ceramic Shield 2 for tougher, more durable glass than what comparable Series 11 models had.

Additionally, there are minor size tweaks with the latest models:

42mm model is 37mm wide, up from Series 11’s 36mm

46mm model is 40mm wide, up from Series 11’s 39mm

The screen size remains the same, but the case being slightly larger results in bigger bezels.

Performance: New S11 chip, double the RAM

There’s a new, more powerful S11 chip in the Apple Watch Series 12, and it’s the first notable performance upgrade since 2023’s S9.

S11 enables new health and AI features that are exclusive to the latest models, as detailed below. Apple doesn’t say what impact it will have on other everyday tasks, but hopefully there’s a noticeable boost there too.

Apple Watch Series 12 also upgrades the memory of the Series 11, offering 4GB of RAM—double the 2GB from last year.

Health: New ‘Health Sensing System’ with key upgrades

With Apple Watch Series 12, Apple is introducing a new “Health Sensing System” that essentially represents an overhaul of the internal sensing components.

In real-world terms, here’s what’s changed and the benefits it brings per Apple:

Heart rate tracking: Second-generation electrical heart sensor and always-on optical heart sensor enable high-frequency background heart rate tracking that you can view on new Heart Rate watch face complication

HRV improvements: “now measured up to 24 times more often and available to view in a new section of the Heart Rate app”

New Recovery HRV: “best for identifying daily signals of stress and recovery”

Step tracking: More accurate, with new Steps complication to track steps in real time from watch face

Software: Audio Intelligence, new Readiness app, and more

It’s not often that new Apple Watch hardware comes with exclusive software features. But Apple has a variety of software-related updates that require Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4.

Audio Intelligence is what Apple calls a “brand-new class of Apple Intelligence features” powered by S11. Some features will be available at launch while others arrive in a software update in late 2026. New features include:

Siri Recap: “[creates] high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment.”

Live Rewind: “[helps] users recall what was just said in conversation. A double press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so users can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with.”

Shazam: “instantly detects the music playing around the user and automatically displays the song title and artist’s name on the Music Recognition widget in the Smart Stack”

Sound Recognition: “[alerts] users who are deaf or hard of hearing of important sounds, even when their iPhone isn’t with them. This feature listens for sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, or a baby crying, and uses on-device intelligence to notify users when they’re detected.”

Joining AI features is a new Readiness app powered by Series 12’s overhauled health sensors. Apple says:

Apple Watch Series 12 introduces readiness, a new feature that analyzes a user’s recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score to offer insight into their capacity for the day ahead. Readiness provides a single 0-10 score with a clear, actionable recommendation: Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. This helps a user decide how to take on their day, whether they’re headed into a workday or tackling their training plan.

As mentioned above, Series 12 also adds new watch face complications for tracking your steps and heart rate.

Battery: Faster charging, outdoor workout gains

Apple Watch Series 12 supports faster charging than Series 11, reducing the amount of time you have to go without wearing it. Per Apple:

Apple Watch Series 12: 15 minutes charge gets up to 12 hours battery life

Apple Watch Series 11: 15 minutes charge gets up to 8 hours battery life

Additionally, while overall quoted battery life is still 24 hours this year, you can now get up to 10 hours of battery during an outdoor workout. That’s 25 percent more than Series 11 supported.

Connectivity: GPS improvement

There’s one more small change: Apple’s website says that Series 12 features “Precision L1 GPS.” 

By contrast, Apple Watch Series 11 only features “GPS.” Adopting the L1 frequency band should enable Apple Watch Series 12 to deliver better GPS precision than before.

Apple Watch Series 12 is now available to pre-order at $399. It ships Friday, September 18.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Shelly’s Flood S Gen4 is a low cost Matter leak sensor for Apple Home
snippet: Water damage is one of those problems where a single sensor can save you a major repair bill on your floors, cabinets, etc. Leak sensors have been among the best values in the smart home for years, and Shelly’s new Flood S Gen4 makes it even easier to get started. It’s under $30, Matter-certified, and works with Apple Home out of the box. more…
fullText:
Water damage is one of those problems where a single sensor can save you a major repair bill on your floors, cabinets, etc. Leak sensors have been among the best values in the smart home for years, and Shelly’s new Flood S Gen4 makes it even easier to get started. It’s under $30, Matter-certified, and works with Apple Home out of the box.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Bigger sensors

Most leak sensors on the market today use small metal pins on the bottom, which means water has to pool in exactly the right spot before anything triggers. Shelly went a different direction with its new sensor, with three large stainless steel pads spread across the bottom of the unit. A larger contact area means water is detected faster and in more places, which is the whole point of putting a sensor under a water heater or washing machine in the first place.

The pads are also sensitive enough to detect clean or low-conductivity water, such as AC condensate. These leaks are often a lot harder to detect. The Flood S Gen4 is also low profile enough to slide under appliances, behind toilets, and beneath sinks, which is exactly where you want these things to live.

Matter/Apple Home support

The Flood S Gen4 is Matter certified and supports Wi-Fi and Zigbee, so it works with Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, SmartThings, and Home Assistant. Once it’s in Apple Home, the automation possibilities open up:

Cut power to a washing machine or dishwasher the moment water is detected (if it’s on a smart outlet)

Trigger every smart bulb in your house

Simple alerts to your iPhone of a leak detected (incredibly helpful if out of town)

Modes, alarms, and battery life

There’s a built-in local alarm alongside the phone notification, so anyone actually in the house hears it even if their phone is in another room. Shelly includes two operating modes, flood detection and rain detection, plus three alarm profiles (intense, normal, and economic) that let you balance a leak detection speed against battery life. It runs up to two years on the included CR123A battery.

Wrap up

At under $30, this is the kind of accessory you buy 3-4 of without thinking. In front of the water heater, in front of the dishwasher, under the washing machine, and under the kitchen sink. Matter/Apple Home support lets you get alerts from the Home app and build your Apple Home automations around it. There’s a lot to like here, and nothing I don’t like. Trust me, a water sensor detector is the smartest investment you can buy for a smart home.

You can buy the Shelly Flood S Gen4 from Amazon or directly from Shelly.

title: This $26 Sliding Pizza Peel Promises to Improve Your Launches, but Does It?
snippet: Here’s my take after testing.
fullText:
Chances are, if you own a pizza oven, have stood near a pizza oven or have uttered the words “pizza oven” in the vicinity of your phone, it’s likely that the almighty algorithm has delivered up a steady stream of pizza oven accessories, from pizza oven stands to sizzler platters to pizza peels in every style and shape.

If you have cursed in the vicinity of your phone while trying to launch a pizza into your pizza oven without inadvertently creating a calzone, chances are even better that Big Internet Brother has targeted you for a sliding pizza peel. If, after dozens of practice launches, you haven’t mastered the art of the traditional wood or perforated metal pizza peel, even with all-powerful semolina flour gliders, you may be very tempted by the ease promised by such a tool as a sliding pizza peel.

	

			

	

			

									

						The Best Pizza Ovens, Tested by CNET					

							

		

But is it worth it? Or is it just the Temu-niverse capitalizing on your desire for a homemade pizza that doesn’t come with a side of anxiety and despair? Reader, the temptation was too strong. I checked one out, and here’s the lowdown on what you can expect from a sliding pizza peel.

How does a sliding pizza peel work?

A sliding pizza peel costs $30 to $40 on Amazon.Pamela Vachon/CNET

A sliding pizza peel is essentially a lightweight wooden pizza peel with a manual conveyor belt attached. Rather than thrusting a stationary peel under your entire pie, you only need a small edge of maneuverability to start. Once the sliding peel gets a little purchase on the raw pizza dough, you pull the cloth slide toward you by its handle while pushing the wooden board underneath. 

To launch the pizza with a sliding pizza peel, reverse the process: Use the handle on the cloth glider to push, sliding the pizza into the oven while pulling the sturdy board out from underneath it.

Cloth, you say? Well, not exactly. The conveyor mechanism moves like fabric, but think of it more like a nonstick baking mat. Many are made of woven fiberglass with a polytetrafluoroethylene coating, which is nonstick but still grips enough to hold raw or cooked pizza dough. It’s frankly like a flimsier Silpat or not unlike an oilcloth table covering.

PTFE, in case you’re wondering, is related to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. Yes, we’ve worked hard to avoid PFAS; however, the material’s pliability doesn’t encourage chipping, and it is also replaceable. The wooden board itself admittedly also spares every expense without the heavy lifting required of other wooden pizza peels — this is made from raw, lightweight bamboo. 

Sliding pizza peel best practices

I practiced with naked dough.Pamela Vachon/CNET

While a sliding pizza peel may seem like a cure-all, if, like me, you adore what your pizza oven offers but still struggle with pizza peel mechanics, it does require some practice of its own — and some caution. As with more traditional pizza peels, it cannot undo other mistakes, such as poorly constructed, too warm pizza dough or an overloaded pie. You can still calzone-ify your pizza, even with a sliding pizza peel.

Unlike a traditional pizza peel, which lets you push and pull simultaneously, the sliding pizza peel’s primary handle is also very short, meaning you kind of have to get (uncomfortably) close to the mouth of the oven to use it.

The fact that none of these seemingly magic wands are produced or branded by any major pizza oven manufacturer should serve as a bit of a caution. (The pizza oven manufacturers probably just want you to become a bona fide pizzaiolo, confidently employing the legitimate tools of the trade; they are clearly not trying to encourage the use of these cheap devices.)

Various sliding pizza peels are purportedly heat-resistant up to a certain temperature (which varies). Many pizza ovens, however, can reach temperatures much hotter than those sliding peels are designed for.

Loading a raw pie into the oven is one of the trickiest parts of at-home pizza making.Pamela Vachon/CNET

More than one user on various online pizza oven forums reported that the nonstick belt of a sliding pizza peel melted onto the hot pizza stone. Others, however, called the device an absolute game changer. Either way, using a sliding pizza peel requires you to launch quickly, which again requires practice, probably best done outside your actual pizza oven. (Your oven-oven with a removable pizza stone? A much lower-stakes practice arena.)

My experience with a sliding pizza peel

Because of the peel’s modest length, you have to get uncomfortably close to the oven during launch.Pamela Vachon/CNET

I have been an enthusiastic pizza oven user since one came into my life, but I still haven’t mastered the mechanics of either a traditional wood or perforated metal pizza peel. I slightly prefer metal, but either way, pizza attempt number one always results in a folded disaster. My crime, apparently, is wanting the kind of thin pizza crust a 20-year-old New Yorker demands. The thinner the pizza, the harder to launch.

I can attest that the sliding pizza peel did make it easy to pull the pizza off the cutting board where I shaped the dough and applied toppings. Despite feeling cheaply made, the mechanics are inarguable. I achieved a crust thinness I truly couldn’t with the other models.

While you have to get close to the heat to deposit it, I haven’t earned any burns or scars from trying. Repeated launches in a very hot pizza oven also didn’t seem to affect the fabric slide, but then again, I was prepared to move extremely fast to avoid a crisis — and to get away from the heat.

Success, if not exactly centered.Pamela Vachion/CNET

In case it merits saying, a sliding pizza peel is entirely unnecessary for pulling pizza out of a pizza oven. In fact, I would caution against it since it really relies on setting the peel down on the pizza stone, never mind the fact that you really have to get your hand inside the oven in the starting position for pulling a pizza onto it. Once a pizza is fully cooked and the dough is sturdy, even a thin pizza can be collected with a more traditional pizza peel anyhow.

A traditional pizza peel is still best for pulling pies from the oven.Pamela Vachon/CNET

The verdict on a sliding pizza peel? Proceed with caution. And practice.

Ultimately, the average price of sliding pizza peels available online is about $30. Even with mixed reviews, it’s a fairly low-stakes gamble to see whether one improves how often you use your big-ticket pizza oven.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Pamela Vachon
						

						

							Contributor						
					

											

								

											Pamela is a freelance food and travel writer based in Astoria, Queens. While she writes about most things edible and potable (and accessories dedicated to those topics,) her real areas of expertise are cheese, chocolate, cooking and wine. She's a culinary school grad, certified sommelier, former bartender and fine dining captain with 10 years in the industry. When not sitting at the keys, she leads in-home cheese classes, wine tastings and cocktail demonstrations.

title: Federico Viticci on iOS 27: ‘It’s good to see Apple sweat the details again’
snippet: Federico Viticci’s annual iOS review is always a must-read over at MacStories, and this year is no different. Federico writes that, while iOS 27 isn’t as “flashy” as last year, the update shows that Apple is “still capable of delivering something new while caring about the old.” more…
fullText:
Federico Viticci’s annual iOS review is always a must-read over at MacStories, and this year is no different. 

Federico writes that, while iOS 27 isn’t as “flashy” as last year, the update shows that Apple is “still capable of delivering something new while caring about the old.” 

I value Federico’s opinion on AI, so I was especially keen to read his thoughts on Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27. Here’s just one small excerpt: 

The new Siri is not an agentic product that is able to carry out long-running tasks to completion, and it would be downright absurd to compare Siri AI to the likes of ChatGPT Work, Claude Cowork, Grok Bot, Hermes Agent, or OpenClaw. I would love for Siri AI to become that kind of experience, and Apple seems to think it now has a foundation in place to enable agentic behavior at some point. But as things stand now, given my reliance on Notion, Slack, and Superhuman for work, and given the simpler, less intelligent nature of Siri AI, I can’t imagine using Apple’s assistant for productivity purposes.

Instead, I’ve come to appreciate Siri AI for what it is – a much better, smarter Siri that doesn’t aim to replace your favorite agent (yet) – without being upset that it’s not something more.

I’ve thoroughly enjoyed using Siri with Apple Notes, Reminders, HomeKit, and third-party apps such as AskPlay, Monologue, Alyx, MusicBox, and LookUp. I’ve found Siri AI to be best at quick, one-off interactions that perhaps involve a couple of follow-ups, but not anything much longer than that. If I realize that a question I have requires deeper research and more back-and-forth, that’s where I fall back to ChatGPT or the excellent Open Minis for iOS.

Federico’s review meticulously covers every detail of iOS 27, with his always-insightful commentary. You can read it over on the MacStories website. Also be sure to read the full MacStories review of macOS 27 Golden Gate and watchOS 27, both written by John Voorhees. Check out the Club MacStories membership program to unlock a whole bunch of extras.

And of course, read along with our coverage of iOS 27 here at 9to5Mac as well. We have roundups of new features, how-tos, guides, and much more.

title: The Galaxy Z Fold 8 needs battery banks that actually fit; iPhone Duo might help
snippet: Magnetic battery banks aren’t everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s hard to argue with the convenience factor they deliver. Samsung’s camera design already makes these difficult on Galaxy devices, but Galaxy Z Fold 8 only makes matters worse with a short form factor that leaves battery banks hanging way over the edge. iPhone Duo might help matters here, but the same old problem remains. more…
fullText:
Magnetic battery banks aren’t everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s hard to argue with the convenience factor they deliver. Samsung’s camera design already makes these difficult on Galaxy devices, but Galaxy Z Fold 8 only makes matters worse with a short form factor that leaves battery banks hanging way over the edge. iPhone Duo might help matters here, but the same old problem remains.

The Qi ring on Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is very low on any already-short frame, which leaves magnetic wallets and battery banks well out of place on the foldable, hanging down below the bottom of the device. It’s a problem begging for a solution, and one that other wide foldables are also going to run into.

Is the iPhone Duo the solution to Samsung’s problem?

Not just yet. The iPhone Duo is bringing about a new wave of smaller Qi2 battery banks to fit the short and stout form factor. BMX just launched one of the first models with a solid-state battery specifically designed to fit the Duo. It has a kickstand ring and a little display to show battery percentage, with 5,000 mAh of power and a fit that doesn’t hang below the bottom edge of Apple’s first foldable.

	

I was hoping this would work on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, but BMX tells 9to5Google that this power bank won’t fit on Samsung’s device due to the camera. Foiled again!

Samsung’s camera design continues to be a problem here, which is why it’s nice that Samsung might be moving to something new on some of its Galaxy S27 devices. But, in the meantime, it remains a problem for existing users.

While BMX says the battery bank won’t fit perfectly on the Fold 8, it’s likely still a major improvement. The $80 power bank is available for purchase now, and it probably won’t be the last battery designed for the Duo and, in turn, a better fit for the Fold 8.

title: Here’s how the iPhone Duo compares to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
snippet: CNET has a series of pieces comparing the iPhone Duo to three current Android foldables. fullText:
CNET has a series of pieces comparing the iPhone Duo to three current Android foldables. While it’s a little frustrating to tackle the comparisons separately, it seems clear that the site views Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 as the device the Duo needs to beat.

That’s in large part because the two devices share similar passport-style aspect ratios rather than the tall and thin design of other foldables, and are priced only $100 apart …

Dimensions

Samsung’s device is a little thinner both when folded and unfolded.

Folded

Unfolded

iPhone Duo

11.3mm

5.2mm

Fold 8

9.7mm

4.5mm

Dust-proofing

One major problem with early versions of Samsung’s foldables is their vulnerability to damage through trapped dust and dirt, and the Fold 8 still has this weakness. Its IP48 rating means that it’s fully waterproof, but only rated against protection from particles larger than a grain of sand. The iPhone Duo, in contrast, is rated as fully waterproof and dustproof.

Cameras

There’s really nothing in it when it comes to the main cameras. The Duo has 48MP main and ultrawide cameras, while those of the Fold 8 are 50MP. Neither device has a telephoto lens.

The Fold 8 has a 10MP selfie camera embedded on the outer display, while the Duo has a 12MP one. Samsung has put another 10 MP selfie camera on the inner display, and while Apple hasn’t revealed the specs on this, it seems to be a significantly lower resolution one based on video shooting supporting 1080p but not 4K.

Battery

As is usual, Apple doesn’t specify the battery capacity, so we’ll need to wait for teardowns to determine this. However, the company says that it will last for up to 24 hours in typical use. 

	

The Fold 8 offers faster wired charging, specifying 0% to 73% in 30 minutes, while Apple says the Duo gets to a 50% charge in the same time. However, Apple wins on wireless charging with full MagSafe support, while the Fold 8 lacks the magnets needed for Qi2 wireless charging.

9to5Mac’s Take

In practice, of course, most people want to remain within their existing ecosystem, be it Apple or Android. Comparisons across operating systems are only relevant when one or other device proves sufficiently appealing to entice people to switch.

My personal suspicion is that the iPhone Duo is better placed than most iPhones when it comes to tempting Android users attracted to the foldable form factor. Samsung’s poor track record with durability could prove critical when choosing such an expensive device – $1900 for the Fold 8 against $1999 for the Duo. Additionally, even Android fans seem to be widely admiring the beauty of Apple’s user interface.

fullText:
Trackers like Apple’s AirTag have been a great piece of added utility to the mobile ecosystem, and every option has a slightly different look and feel. Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is rumored to be launching soon and, thanks to a pair of leaks, we know exactly what to expect.

As pictured below, both prior generations of Galaxy SmartTag have had some sort of built-in loop for mounting, and this is also commonplace among other third-party smarttrackers from the likes of Pebblebee, Chipolo, and more. Apple’s AirTag, Motorola’s Moto Tag, and Google’s upcoming Pixel Tag all lack built-in mounting options too, though.

	

Functionally, this leak also reveals that SmartTag 3 will have UWB and Bluetooth, as well as an IP67 rating and around 500 days of battery life. There’s no mention of what network it will use, but it’s almost certainly exclusive to Samsung’s network rather than using Google’s Find Hub network in any capacity.

The other report claims pricing will be unchanged at €39.99 ($29.99 US), though a 4-pack will go from €129.99 to $139.99 this time around.

title: India escalates Apple probe over alleged iOS 18 issues that incurred repair costs
snippet: India’s Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has reportedly escalated its probe into whether Apple should be held responsible for an iOS 18 update that allegedly caused display and microphone issues on some iPhones. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
India’s Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has reportedly escalated its probe into whether Apple should be held responsible for an iOS 18 update that allegedly caused display and microphone issues on some iPhones. Here are the details.

Apple faces yet another probe in India

As reported by Reuters, Apple is facing renewed regulatory scrutiny over the iOS 18 update, from 2024.

According to the country’s CCPA, the update allegedly “​led to screen display and microphone malfunctions among other issues, forcing customers to pay for related repairs, as no warranty is provided on software,” says Reuters.

Apple has denied the allegations, while also stressing that not offering a warranty for software issues is standard industry practice. Still, the CCPA is unconvinced and has recently escalated the matter to its investigation wing for a more detailed probe.

Here’s Reuters:

If found guilty, Apple may have to pay fines but more importantly could be ​forced to issue refunds or make changes to its business practices.

Reuters says the investigation covers complaints from users who reported green, pink, or white lines appearing on their iPhone displays after installing iOS 18.

Apple, meanwhile, says the case is based on just 75 complaints and that it found no systemic issues or safety concerns with iOS 18 in India. Apple further argues that requiring every software-related problem to be covered by warranty “would effectively ⁠convert any software provider into an insurer against all technological risk.”

The CCPA, however, argues that the issue goes beyond the number of individual complaints, accusing Apple of violating the rights of “consumers as a class.” The regulator also says that charging customers for repairs due to problems allegedly caused by Apple’s own software could amount to an unfair trade practice.

This probe is just one of several recent spats between Apple and Indian regulators, as the company is also fighting the Competition Commission of India (CCI) over an App Store antitrust case that could potentially result in a $38 billion fine.

Separately, Apple has repeatedly pushed back against Indian government orders requiring smartphone makers to pre-install a state-run app on devices sold in the country, while one of its major suppliers, Tata, recently faced scrutiny from local regulators over alleged wastewater contamination at an iPhone component plant.

fullText:
Last week, Apple announced an iPhone unlike any it has made in the past. An iPhone that has seemingly already led several other phone manufacturers to pursue entirely different designs for their flagship products. A remarkably distinct device with the kind of “I can’t believe they did that” software touches that Apple sometimes pulls off when it’s at the top of its game.

That phone is not the iPhone 18 Pro.

The 18 Pro and Pro Max are in the unusual position of being the second-most interesting iPhones that Apple is launching this year. The foldable iPhone Duo stole the show at Apple’s launch event, but it’s not arriving until next month. In the meantime, the 18 Pro cometh, and it is extremely familiar even with a totally new hardware feature in the camera.

It is so similar to the iPhone 17 Pro that it can use the same cases. Have you used an iPhone 17 Pro? Great, you now know what it’s like to use the 18 Pro. There are no surprises, and unless you’re a truly committed smartphone photographer, no hugely compelling reason to pick an 18 Pro over a 17 Pro if you can find one on sale. It’s what we’ve come to expect from what was the flagship iPhone: excellent and utterly iterative.

8
